SECTION 22 of Apprentices Act, 1961
Apprentices Act, 1961
22. OFFER 

AND ACCEPTANCE OF EMPLOYMENT. -
(1) It shall 

not be obligatory on the part of the employer to offer any employment to any 

apprentice who has completed the period of his apprenticeship training in his 

establishment, nor shall it be obligatory on the part of the apprentice to 

accept an employment under the employer.
(2) 

Notwithstanding anything in sub-section (1), where there is a condition in a 

contract of apprenticeship shall, after the successful completion of the 

apprenticeship training, serve the employer, the employer shall, on such 

completion, be bound to offer suitable employment to the apprentice, and the 

apprentice shall be bound to serve the employer in that capacity for such period 

and on such remuneration as may be specified in the contract :
Provided that where 

such period or remuneration is not, in the opinion of the Apprenticeship 

Adviser, reasonable, he may revise such period or remuneration so as to make it 

reasonable, and the period or remuneration so revised shall be deemed to be the 

period or remuneration agreed to between the apprentice and the employer.
Comments:

 

What is indeed required is to see that nation gets the benefit of time, money 

and energy spend on the trainees, which would be so when they are employed in  

preference to  non-trained direct recruits. This would also meet the 

legitimate expectations of the trainees. U.P. State Road Transport 

Corporation v. U.P. Parivahan Nigam Shishukhs Berozgar Sangh AIR 1995 SUPREME 

COURT 1115
simplified_text:
Simplified text:  Offer and Acceptance of Employment:
Employer's Choice: Employers are not required to offer employment to apprentices once they complete their training, and similarly, apprentices are not obligated to accept any job offered by the employer.
Contract Conditions: However, if there is a specific condition in the apprenticeship agreement that states the apprentice must work for the employer after completing training, then the employer must offer suitable employment to the apprentice. The apprentice, in turn, must serve the employer in that role for the designated period and at the specified salary mentioned in the contract. If the period or salary prescribed in the contract is deemed unreasonable by the Apprenticeship Adviser, they have the authority to adjust these terms to a reasonable level. The revised terms will then be considered agreed upon by both the apprentice and the employer.

Comment:
The aim is to ensure that the time, money, and effort invested in training apprentices benefit the nation by giving priority to employing them over non-trained recruits. This approach aligns with the justified expectations of the trainees.

SECTION 32 of Apprentices Act, 1961

32. OFFENCES 

BY COMPANIES. -
(1) If the 

person committing an offence under this Act is a company, every person who, at 

the time the offence was committed was in charge of, and was responsible to, the 

company for the conduct of business of the company, as well as the company, 

shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded 

against and punished accordingly :
Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any such person liable 

to such punishment provided in this Act if he proves that the offence was 

committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to 

prevent the commission of such offence.
(2) 

Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where an offence under 

this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has 

been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to any 

negligence on the part of, any director, manager, secretary or other officer of 

the company, such director, manager, secretary, or other officer shall also be 

deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against 

and punished accordingly.
Explanation 

:  

For the purposes of this section, -
(a) 

"company" means a body corporate and includes a firm or other association of 

individuals; and
(b) 

"director" in relation to a firm means a partner in the firm.

If a company commits an offence under this law, both the company and any person in charge of the company's business at that time will be considered guilty of the offence. They can be prosecuted and punished for it. However, if the person proves that they had no knowledge of the offence or took all necessary steps to prevent it, they may not be punished.

Additionally, if it's proven that the offence was committed with the consent, knowledge, or negligence of a director, manager, secretary, or other company officer, they will also be held accountable and can face punishment.

Definition:
- "Company" refers to a corporation or any group of individuals working together.
- In the case of a firm, a "director" is considered a partner in that firm.

Simplified text:

Conditions for Enforcing Foreign Awards:
For a foreign award to be enforced under this law, it must meet the following criteria:

1. It must be based on a valid arbitration agreement according to the governing law.
2. It should be issued by the agreed tribunal or in the manner the parties have arranged.
3. It must follow the arbitration procedure's governing law.
4. The award must be final in the country where it was issued.
5. The subject matter must be capable of being resolved through arbitration under the law.
6. Enforcement should not violate public policy or local law.

Non-Enforceable Situations:
A foreign award cannot be enforced under this law if:

1. It has been annulled in the issuing country.
2. The party to whom enforcement is sought didn't receive proper notice of the arbitration proceedings or was unable to present their case.
3. The award doesn't cover all the matters referred to or includes decisions beyond the arbitration agreement's scope.

Challenging Enforceability:
If a party wants to resist enforcing a foreign award and can show grounds beyond those mentioned above, the Court may refuse enforcement or delay it to allow the concerned party time to challenge the award's validity.

Definitions:

agreement" means an agreement by the parties to submit to arbitration all

Arbitration Agreement: 
An "arbitration agreement" in this part refers to an agreement where the parties agree to resolve certain or all disputes that have arisen or may arise between them regarding a specific legal relationship, regardless of whether it is based on a contract.
Form of Agreement: 
The arbitration agreement can be a clause within a contract or a separate agreement.
Written Agreement: 
For an arbitration agreement to be valid, it must be in writing and can be:
- A signed document by the involved parties.
- Correspondence like letters, telex, telegrams, or other telecommunication methods that confirm the agreement.
- A set of statements detailing claims and defenses where one party asserts the existence of the agreement and the other party does not deny it.
Reference in Contract:

Simplified text: Appointment of Arbitrators:

Who Can Be an Arbitrator:
Anyone from any country can be an arbitrator, unless the parties agree otherwise.

Agreement on Appointing Arbitrators:
The parties can decide how to choose the arbitrator(s) unless they have already agreed on a specific process.

Procedure for Choosing Arbitrators:
If there are three arbitrators, each party picks one and those two together choose a third arbitrator to lead.
If a party doesn’t choose an arbitrator within 30 days or if the two chosen arbitrators can't agree on the third one within 30 days, the Chief Justice or a designated person can make the appointment upon request.


In the case of a single arbitrator, if the parties can't agree on one within 30 days, the Chief Justice or a designated person can make the appointment upon request.


Failure to Follow Agreed Procedure:
If a party or the appointed arbitrators don't follow the agreed procedure, the Chief Justice or a designated person can step in to ensure the appointment.



Qualifications and Impartiality:
The Chief Justice or designated person considers the arbitrator's qualifications and independence when making appointments.



International Commercial Arbitration:
In international cases, the Chief Justice or designated person can appoint an arbitrator from a different nationality if the parties are from different countries.



Final Decisions:
Decisions made by the Chief Justice or designated person regarding arbitrator appointments are final.



Handling Requests:
The Chief Justice can establish a system to manage requests related to arbitrator appointments.


Authority of Chief Justice:
If multiple requests are made to different Chief Justices, the first Chief Justice or their designate to receive the request will be the one to decide.

Note: The Chief Justice in international commercial cases refers to the Chief Justice of India, while in other cases, it refers to the Chief Justice of the High Court where the main Civil Court is located.

(1) When a person is approached in connection

independence or impartiality.
(2) An arbitrator, from the time of his

(1) unless they have already been informed of them by him.
(3) An arbitrator may be challenged only if -
(a)  circumstances 

exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his independence or

impartiality, or
(b)  he 

does not possess the qualifications agreed to by the parties.
(4) A party may challenge an arbitrator

appointed by him, or in whose appointment he has participated, only for reasons

of which he becomes aware after the appointment has been made.

1. When a person is being considered for appointment as an arbitrator, they must disclose in writing any information that could raise doubts about their independence or impartiality.
2. An arbitrator must promptly inform all parties in writing about any relevant circumstances that could affect their neutrality, from the time of their appointment and throughout the arbitration process.
3. An arbitrator can only be challenged if:
   - There are circumstances that cast doubt on their independence or impartiality, or
   - They do not possess the qualifications agreed upon by the parties.
4. A party can challenge an arbitrator chosen by them, or in whose selection they were involved, only if they learn of reasons to challenge the arbitrator after the appointment is finalized.

SECTION 13 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 13
Challenge Procedure.
(1) Subject to sub-section (4), the parties are

free to agree on a procedure for challenging an arbitrator.

upon by the parties or under the procedure under sub-section (2) is not

successful, the arbitral tribunal shall continue the arbitral proceedings and

make an arbitral award.

**Termination of Arbitrator's Role:**

SECTION 16 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 16
Competence of Arbitral tribunal to Rule on its Jurisdiction
(1) The arbitral tribunal may rule on its own

jurisdiction, including ruling on any objections with respect to the existence

or validity of the arbitration agreement, and for that purpose, -
(a)  an 

arbitration clause which forms part of a contract shall be treated as an

agreement independent of the other terms of the contract; and
(b)  a 

decision by the arbitral tribunal that the contract is null and void shall not

entail ipso  jure  the invalidity of the arbitration

clause.
(2) A plea that the arbitral tribunal does not

have jurisdiction shall be raised not later than the submission of the

statement of defense; however, a party shall not be precluded from raising such

a plea merely because that he has appointed, or participated in the appointment

of an arbitrator.
(3) A plea that the arbitral tribunal is

exceeding the scope of its authority shall be raised as soon as the matter

alleged to be beyond the scope of its authority is raised during the arbitral

proceedings.
(4) The arbitral tribunal may, in either of

the cases referred to in sub-section (2) or sub-section (3), admit a later plea

if it considers the delay justified.
(5) The arbitral tribunal shall decide on a

plea referred to in sub-section (2) or sub-section (3) and, where the arbitral

tribunal takes a decision rejecting the plea, continue with the arbitral

proceedings and make an arbitral award.
(6) A party aggrieved by such an arbitral

award may make an application for setting aside such an arbitral award in

accordance with section 34.

Simplified text: Arbitration Tribunal's Jurisdiction
The arbitration tribunal has the authority to decide on its own jurisdiction, including any objections about the validity of the arbitration agreement. In this regard:
- An arbitration clause in a contract is considered separate from the other contract terms.
- If the tribunal determines that the contract is invalid, it does not automatically invalidate the arbitration clause.
Challenges on Jurisdiction: Any objection regarding the tribunal's jurisdiction must be raised when submitting the defense statement. If the tribunal is believed to be exceeding its authority, the objection should be raised promptly during the arbitration proceedings.
Admitting Delayed Objections: The tribunal may consider late objections if there is a valid reason for the delay.
Decision and Award: The tribunal will make a decision on jurisdiction challenges, and if it rejects the objection, it will proceed with the arbitration and issue an award. If a party is unhappy with the award, they can seek to set it aside following the procedures outlined in section 34.

Section 24
Hearings and Written Proceedings

the arbitral tribunal shall decide whether to hold oral hearings for the

presentation of evidence or for oral argument, or whether the proceedings shall

SECTION 27 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 27
Court Assistance in taking Evidence
(1) The arbitral tribunal, or a party with the

approval of the arbitral tribunal, may apply to the Court for assistance in

taking evidence.
(2) The application shall specify -
(a)  the 

names and addresses of the parties and the arbitrators,
(b)  the 

general nature of the claim and the relief sought;
(c)  the 

evidence to be obtained, in particular, -
( i )

 the  name and address of any person to be heard as

witness or expert witness and a statement
of  the subject matter of

the testimony required;
(ii)  the  description of any document to the produced or property

to be inspected.
(3) The Court may, within its competence and

according to its rules on taking evidence, execute the request by ordering that

the evidence be provided directly to the arbitral tribunal.
(4) The Court may, while making an order under

sub-section (3), issue the same processes to witnesses as it may issue in suits

tried before it.
(5) Persons failing to attend in accordance

with such process, or making any other default, or refusing to give their

evidence, or guilty of any contempt to the arbitral tribunal during the conduct

of arbitral proceedings, shall be subject to the like disadvantages, penalties

and punishments by order of the Court on the representation of the arbitral

tribunal as they would incur for the like offences in suits tried before the

Court.
(6) In this section the expression

"Processes" includes summonses and commissions for the examination of

witnesses and summonses to produce documents.

SECTION 28 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 28
Rules Applicable to Substance of Dispute
(1) Where the place of arbitration is situate

in India  , -

tribunal shall decide the dispute submitted to arbitration in accordance with

the substantive law for the time being in force in India  ;

SECTION 31 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 31
Form and Contents of Arbitral Award
(1) An arbitral award shall be made in writing

and shall be signed by the members of the arbitral tribunal.
(2) For the purposes of sub-section (1), in

arbitral proceedings with more than one arbitrator, the signatures of the

majority of all the members of the arbitral tribunal shall be sufficient so

long as the reason for any omitted signature is stated.
(3) The arbitral award shall state the reasons

upon which it is based, unless -
(a)  the 

parties have agreed that no reasons are to be given, or
(b)  the 

award is an arbitral award on agreed terms under section 30.
(4) The arbitral award shall state its date

and the place of arbitration as determined in accordance with section 20 and

the award shall be deemed to have been made at that place.
(5) After the arbitral award is made, a signed

copy shall be delivered to each party.
(6) The arbitral tribunal may, at any time

during the arbitral proceedings, make an interim arbitral award on any matter

with respect to which it may make a final arbitral award.
(7) (a) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties,

where and in so far as an arbitral award is for the payment of money, the

arbitral tribunal may include in the sum for which the award is made interest,

at such rate as it deems reasonable, on the whole or any part of the money, for

the whole or any part of the period between the date on which the cause of

action arose and the date on which the award is made.
(b) A sum directed to

be paid by an arbitral award shall, unless the award otherwise directs, carry

interest at the rate of eighteen per centum per annum from the date of the

award to the date of payment.
(8) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, -
(a)  the 

costs of an arbitration shall be fixed by the arbitral tribunal;
(b)  the 

arbitral tribunal shall specify -
( i )

 the  party entitled to costs,
(ii)  the  party who shall pay the costs,
(iii)  the  amount of costs or method of determining that amount,

and
(iv)  the  manner in which the costs shall be paid.
Explanation:

For the purpose of

clause (a), "costs" means reasonable costs relating to -
( i )  the  fees and expenses of the arbitrators and witnesses,
(ii)  legal  fees and

expenses,
(iii)  any 

administration fees of the institution supervising the arbitration, and
(iv)  any  other

expenses incurred in connection with the arbitral proceedings and the arbitral

award.
Comment: Thus, the law on the award, as governed by

the new Act, is other way about of the preexisting law; it mandates that the

award should state the reasons upon which it is based. In other words, unless

(a) the parties have agreed that no reasons are to be given or (b) the award is

an arbitral award on agreed terms under Section 30 of the New Act, the award

should state the reasons in support of determination of the

liability/non-liability. Thereby, legislature has not accepted the ratio of the

Constitution Bench in the  Chokhamal  Contractor's case

(AIR 1990 SC 1426), that the award, being in the private law field, need not be

a speaking award even where the award relates to the contract of private parties

or between person and the Government or public sector undertakings. The

principle is the same, namely the award is governed by Section 31(3).  T.N.

Electricity Board v. M/s. Bridge Tunnel Constructions, AIR 1997 SUPREME COURT

1376
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Form and Content of Arbitration Award:

1. Written Requirement:
An arbitration award must be in writing and signed by all arbitration tribunal members. If there are multiple arbitrators, a majority signature is enough as long as reasons are provided for any missing signatures.

2. Reasoning:
The award must include the reasons behind its decision, unless the parties agree otherwise or the award is made based on agreed terms.

3. Date and Location:
The award should mention the date and the place of arbitration, as determined under section 20, with delivery of a signed copy to each party.

4. Interim Awards:
The tribunal can issue interim awards during proceedings, addressing matters that may also be finalized in a final award.

5. Interest and Costs:
Interest on monetary awards can be included, as determined by the tribunal. Costs of arbitration should be decided by the arbitral tribunal, outlining who pays, how much, and in what manner.

6. Definitions:
Costs include arbitrator and witness fees, legal expenses, administration fees, and other expenses related to the arbitration process and award.

7. Explanation:
The law now requires award reasoning unless agreed otherwise, contrary to past practices. This ensures transparency and accountability in the arbitration process.

SECTION 33 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 33
Correction and Interpretation of Award; Additional Award
(1) Within thirty days from the receipt of the

arbitral award, unless another period of time has been agreed upon by the

parties -
(a)  a 

party, with notice to the other party, may request the arbitral tribunal to

correct any computation errors, any clerical or typographical errors or any

other errors of a similar nature occurring in the award;
(b)  if 

so agreed by the parties, a party, with notice to the other party, may request

the arbitral tribunal to give an interpretation of a specific point or part of

the award.
(2) If the arbitral tribunal considers the

request made under sub-section (1) to be justified, it shall make the

correction or give the interpretation within thirty days from the receipt of

the request and the interpretation shall form part of the arbitral award.
(3) The arbitral tribunal may correct any

error of the type referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (1), on its own

initiative, within thirty days from the date of the arbitral award.
(4) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, a

party with notice to the other  party,  may request,

within thirty days from the receipt of the arbitral award, the arbitral

tribunal to make an additional arbitral award as to claims presented in the

arbitral proceedings but omitted from the arbitral award.
(5) If the arbitral tribunal considers the

request made under sub-section (4) to be justified, it shall make the

additional arbitral award within sixty days from the receipt of such request.
(6) The arbitral tribunal may extend, if

necessary, the period of time within which it shall make a correction, give an

interpretation or make an additional arbitral award under sub-section (2) or sub-section

(5).
(7) Section 31 shall apply to a correction or

interpretation of the arbitral award or to an  

additional  arbitral made under this section.
simplified_text:
Simplified text:
Correction and Interpretation of Award:
Quick Actions Needed: Within 30 days of receiving the arbitral award, a party can ask the arbitral tribunal to correct errors like miscalculations, typos, or similar mistakes. The tribunal can also clarify specific points in the award if both parties agree.

Timely Resolutions: If the tribunal agrees that changes are needed, they must be made within 30 days. Any interpretation given becomes part of the final award.

Additional Award Requests: Within 30 days of getting the award, a party can ask the tribunal for a new award on claims that were missed in the original proceedings, if not agreed otherwise. The tribunal has 60 days to issue this new award if deemed necessary.

Flexibility: The tribunal can extend the time limits for corrections, interpretations, or new awards if required.

Legal provisions: Section 31 of the Arbitration Act applies to corrections, interpretations, and additional awards made under this section.

SECTION 34 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 34
Application for Setting Aside Arbitral Award
(1) Recourse to a Court against an arbitral

award may be made only by an application for setting aside such award in

accordance with sub-section (2) and sub-section (3).
(2) An arbitral award may be set aside by the

Court only if -
(a)  the 

party making the application furnishes proof that -
( i )

 a  party was under some incapacity, or
(ii)  the  arbitration agreement is not valid under the law to

which the parties have subjected it or, failing any indication thereon, under

the law for the time being in force; or
(iii) the party making

the application was not given proper notice of the appointment of an arbitrator

or of the arbitral proceedings or was otherwise unable to present his case; or
(iv) the arbitral

award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms

of the submission to arbitration, or it contains decisions on matters beyond

the scope of the submission to  arbitration : Provided

that, if the decisions on matters submitted to arbitration can be separated

from those not so submitted, only that part of the arbitral award which

contains decisions on matters not submitted to arbitration may be set aside; or


(v) the composition of

the arbitral tribunal or the arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the

agreement of the parties, unless such agreement was in conflict with a

provision of this Part from which the parties cannot derogate, or, failing such

agreement, was not in accordance with this Part; or
(b)  the 

Court finds that -
( i )

 the  subject-matter of the dispute is not capable of

settlement by arbitration under the law for the time being in force, or
(ii)  the  arbitral award is in conflict with the public policy of

India.
Explanation :

 Without prejudice to

the generality of sub-clause (ii), it is hereby declared, for the avoidance of

any doubt, that an award is in conflict with the public policy of India if the

making of the award was induced or affected by fraud or corruption or was in

violation of section 75 or section 81.
(3) An application for setting aside may not

be made after three months have elapsed from the date on which the party making

that application had received the arbitral award or, if a request had been made

under section 33, from the date on which that request had been disposed of by

the arbitral tribunal :
Provided that if the Court is satisfied that the

applicant was prevented by sufficient cause from making the application within

the said period of three months it may entertain the application within a further

period of thirty days, but not thereafter.
(4) On receipt of an application under

sub-section (1), the Court may, where it is appropriate and it is so request by

a party, adjourn the proceedings for a period of time determined by it in order

to give the arbitral tribunal an opportunity to resume the arbitral proceedings

or to take such take action as in the opinion of arbitral tribunal will

eliminate the grounds for setting aside the arbitral award.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: 

Application for Challenging an Arbitral Award: 

A party can challenge an arbitral award by submitting an application to set it aside, following the conditions outlined below.

Grounds for Setting Aside an Award:

1. The award can only be set aside by a court if:
   a. The party applying proves that:
      i. A party was incapable.
      ii. The arbitration agreement is invalid under the agreed-upon law or the prevailing law.
      iii. Proper notice wasn't given, preventing a fair case presentation.
      iv. The award covers a dispute beyond the arbitration agreement.
      v. The tribunal's composition or procedure didn't meet party agreement.
   b. The Court determines that:
      i. The dispute isn't suitable for arbitration under current law.
      ii. The award violates India's public policy.

Time Limit for Challenging:
- The application must be made within three months of receiving the award (or its disposal under section 33) unless a valid reason delays this. In such cases, an additional thirty-day period may be granted.

Court Proceedings:
- Upon receiving the application, the Court may postpone proceedings if requested, allowing the tribunal time to address issues to remedy the grounds for setting aside the award.

SECTION 38 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 38
Deposits
(1) The arbitral tribunal may fix the amount

of the deposit or supplementary deposit, as the case may be, as an advance for

the costs referred to in sub-section (8) of section 31, which it expects will

be incurred in respect of the claim submitted to  it :
Provided that where, apart from the claim, a

counter-claim has been submitted to the arbitral tribunal, it may fix separate

amount of deposit for the claim and counter-claim.
(2) The deposit referred to in sub-section (1)

shall be payable in equal shares by the  parties :
Provided that where one party fails to pay his share

of the deposit, the other party may pay that  share :
Provided further that where the other party also

does not pay the aforesaid share in respect of the claim or the counter-claim,

the arbitral tribunal may suspend or terminate the arbitral proceedings in

respect of such claim or counter-claim, as the case may be.
(3) Upon termination of the arbitral

proceedings, the arbitral tribunal shall render an accounting to the parties of

the deposits received and shall return any unexpended balance to the party or

parties, as the case may be.

Simplified text: 
Deposits in Arbitration:
1. Fixing Deposit: The arbitration tribunal can decide on the amount of money to be deposited in advance to cover expected costs related to the claim being dealt with.
2. Payment Sharing: The deposit amount must be split equally between the parties involved. If one party fails to pay their share, the other party may cover it. If a party doesn't pay their share for the claim or counter-claim, the tribunal can pause or end the arbitration process for that particular claim.
3. Return of Unspent Funds: At the end of the arbitration process, the tribunal will provide a report on the deposits received and return any leftover funds to the relevant party/parties.

SECTION 39 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 39
Lien on Arbitral Award and Deposits as to Costs
(1) Subject to the provisions of sub-section

(2) and to any provision to the contrary in the arbitration agreement, the arbitral

tribunal shall have a lien on the arbitral award for any unpaid costs of the

arbitration.
(2) If in any case an arbitral tribunal

refuses to deliver its award except on payment of the costs demanded by it, the

Court may, on an application in this behalf, order that the arbitral tribunal

shall deliver the arbitral award to the applicant on payment into Court by the

applicant of the costs demanded, and shall, after such inquiry, if any, as it

thinks fit, further order that out of the money so paid into Court there shall

be paid to the arbitral tribunal by way of costs such sum as the Court may

consider reasonable and that the balance of the money, if any, shall be

refunded to the applicant.
(3) An application under sub-section (2) may

be made by any party unless the fees demanded have been fixed by written

agreement between him and the arbitral tribunal, and the arbitral tribunal

shall be entitled to appear and be heard on any such application.
(4) The Court may make such orders as it

thinks fit respecting the costs of the arbitration where any question arises

respecting such costs and the arbitral award contains no sufficient provision

concerning them.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Lien on Arbitral Award and Deposits for Costs
Unpaid Costs: The arbitration tribunal has a right to keep hold of the arbitral award if the costs of the arbitration have not been paid, except when the arbitration agreement says otherwise.
Releasing Award: If the arbitration tribunal refuses to provide the award until the costs are paid, the Court can order the tribunal to give the award to the applicant once the costs are paid to the Court. The Court may decide on a reasonable sum to be paid to the tribunal as costs, with any remaining amount refunded to the applicant.
Application Process: Any party involved can request the Court's intervention unless the fees have been agreed upon in writing. The tribunal is also allowed to present their views in such applications.
Costs Determination: The Court can issue orders regarding the arbitration costs when there is a dispute, and the arbitral award doesn't specify them adequately.

SECTION 41 of Arbitration Act, 1940
Arbitration Act 1940
Section 41
Provisions in Case of Insolvency
(1) Where it is provided by a term in a

contract to which an insolvent is a party that any dispute arising  thereout  or in connection therewith shall be submitted to

arbitration, the said term shall, if the receiver adopts the contract, be

enforceable by or against him so far it as relates to any such dispute.
(2) Where a person who has been adjudged an

insolvent had, before the commencement of the insolvency proceedings, become a

Simplified text: 

Arbitration Jurisdiction:
The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Chapter IV

Competence of Arbitral Tribunals to Decide on Their Jurisdiction:
1. The arbitral tribunal has the authority to determine its own jurisdiction, including deciding on any objections related to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement. For this purpose:
a. An arbitration clause within a contract is considered a separate agreement from the rest of the contract.
b. If the arbitral tribunal declares the contract null and void, it does not automatically invalidate the arbitration clause.

2. A party must raise any objection regarding the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal no later than when submitting their defense statement. However, appointing or taking part in appointing an arbitrator does not prevent a party from raising such an objection.

3. If a party believes the arbitral tribunal is overstepping its authority, this objection must be raised promptly when the issue arises during the arbitration process.

4. The arbitral tribunal has the discretion to accept a late objection if it deems the delay reasonable in cases mentioned in subsections (2) or (3).

5. The arbitral tribunal will decide on jurisdictional objections, and if the objection is rejected, the arbitration will continue, leading to an arbitral award.

6. If a party is dissatisfied with the arbitral award, they can apply to set it aside following the procedures outlined in section 34.

Upon receiving an arbitral award, a party has thirty days to request the arbitral tribunal to correct any calculation, clerical, typographical errors, or similar mistakes found in the award. If agreed upon by both parties, a request for the interpretation of a specific point or part of the award can also be made within this time frame.

   - There was incapacity of a party.

(1) For the purposes of preparing the register

of architects for the first time, the Central Government shall, by notification

in the Official Gazette, constitute a Registration Tribunal consisting of three

persons who have, in the opinion of the Central Government, the knowledge of,

or experience in, architecture; and the Registrar appointed under section 12

before the appointed day and if it is satisfied that the applicant is qualified

for registration under section 25, shall direct the entry of the name of the

applicant in the register.
(4) The first register so prepared shall thereafter be published in such manner

as the Central Government may direct and any person aggrieved by a decision of

the Registration Tribunal expressed or implied in the register so published

may, within thirty days from the date of such publication, appeal against such

decision to an authority appointed by the Central Government in this behalf by

notification in the Official Gazette.
(5) The authority appointed under sub-section

(4) shall, after giving the person affected an opportunity of being heard and

after calling for relevant records, make such order as it may deem fit.
(6) The Registrar shall amend, where

necessary, the register in accordance with the decisions of the authority

appointed under sub-section (4).
(7) Every person whose name is entered in the

register shall be issued a certificate of registration in such form as may be

prescribed by rules.
(8) Upon the constitution of the Council, the

register shall be given into its custody, and the Central Government may direct

that the whole or any specified part of the application fees for registration

in the first register shall be 
paid to the credit of the Council.

The Central Government can create rules by publishing them in the Official Gazette to implement the Architects Act, 1972.

Every rule created must be presented to both Houses of Parliament during a session for a period of thirty days. The Armed Forces (Jammu and Kashmir) Special Powers Act, 1990
3. Power to declare areas to be disturbed areas.-
If, in relation to the State of Jammu and Kashmir*, the Governor of that State or the Central Government, is of opinion that the whole or any part of the State is in such a disturbed and dangerous condition that the use of armed forces in aid of the civil power is necessary to prevent-
(a) activities involving terrorist acts directed towards overawing the Government as by law established or striking terror in the people or any section of the people or alienating any section of the people or adversely affecting the harmony amongst different sections of the people;
(b) activities directed towards disclaiming, questioning or disrupting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of India or bringing about cession of a part of the territory of India or secession of a part of the territory of India from the Union or causing insult to the Indian National Flag, the Indian National Anthem and the Constitution of India, the Governor of the State or the Central Government, may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare the whole or any part of the State to be a disturbed area.
Explanation.- In this section, "terrorist act" has the same meaning as in Explanation to article 248 of the Constitution of India as applicable to the State of Jammu and Kashmir*.
*. Vide notification No. S.O. 3912(E), dated 30th October, 2019, this Act is made applicable to the Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir and the Union territory of Ladakh.

Simplified text: Special Powers of the Armed Forces in Disturbed Areas

In areas of unrest, certain ranks within the armed forces are allowed to take specific actions to maintain public order. These include:

A. Use of Force: If deemed necessary for public order, they can use force, including firing upon individuals, if they are violating laws prohibiting assemblies or carrying weapons.

B. Destruction: They can destroy weapon stockpiles, fortified positions, or shelters used for armed attacks or training camps, and hideouts of armed groups.

C. Arrest: They can arrest individuals without a warrant if they are suspected of committing or about to commit a crime, and can use force as necessary.

D. Search and Seizure: They can enter premises without a warrant to arrest suspects, recover stolen property, or seize illegal weapons or substances, using force if needed.

E. Stop and Search: They can stop, search, and seize vehicles or vessels if there are suspicions of carrying offenders or illegal items, using force as necessary.

Simplified text: Special Powers of Armed Forces:
In an area facing disturbances, any officer, warrant officer, non-commissioned officer, or a person with equivalent rank in the armed forces can take the following actions if necessary for maintaining public order:

Fire upon or use force, including lethal force, after giving a warning, against individuals violating laws or orders in the disturbed area that prohibit gatherings of 5 or more people, carrying weapons, or possessing firearms, ammunition, or explosives.

Destroy arms dumps, fortified positions, shelters used for armed attacks, training camps for armed volunteers, or hideouts for criminals.

Arrest individuals without a warrant who have committed or are suspected of committing a crime, using force if necessary.

Enter and search premises without a warrant to make arrests, rescue restrained individuals, recover stolen property, or seize illegal weapons, ammunition, or explosive substances, using force if required.

Stop, search, and seize vehicles or vessels suspected of carrying proclaimed offenders, individuals involved in non-serious offenses, or possessing illegal weapons, ammunition, or explosives, using necessary force for these actions.

Simplified text: Jurisdiction and Procedures of the Armed Forces Tribunal

Jurisdiction in Service Matters:

The Armed Forces Tribunal shall have the authority to handle all service-related matters. This involves the powers and jurisdiction previously held by all courts, excluding the Supreme Court or High Courts dealing with matters under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution.

Application Process:

Individuals affected by a service-related order can file an application with the Tribunal. The application should include necessary documents and evidence, along with the prescribed fee.

Adjudication Process:

Upon receiving an application concerning service matters, the Tribunal will assess its suitability for adjudication. If deemed appropriate, the application will be accepted; if not, it may be dismissed with reasons provided.

Powers of the Tribunal:

The Tribunal is empowered to perform various functions similar to those of a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. This includes summoning persons for testimony, requesting document production, and receiving evidence via affidavits. Additionally, the Tribunal can issue commissions for witness examinations, review decisions, and handle other matters as specified by the Central Government.

Decisions on Legal and Factual Issues:

The Tribunal is responsible for deciding on both legal questions and factual issues raised during proceedings before it.

Simplified text: Jurisdiction of the Armed Forces Tribunal

The Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007 gives the Armed Forces Tribunal specific jurisdiction:

1. From the designated day, the Tribunal will have all the authority to handle appeals against rulings made by a court martial or related matters under this Act, unless stated otherwise.
2. Anyone unhappy with a court martial's ruling can file an appeal following the specified procedures.
3. The Tribunal can decide to provide bail to a person in military custody, with or without conditions, except for serious offenses like those punishable by death or life imprisonment.
4. The Tribunal can allow an appeal against conviction by a court martial if the ruling is legally unsound, involves a wrong legal decision, or there were trial irregularities leading to a miscarriage of justice. If no injustice is likely or occurred, the appeal may be dismissed, with reasons given in writing.
5. The Tribunal can allow an appeal against conviction and issue an appropriate decision.
6. The Tribunal has the authority to substitute or modify a court martial's findings and sentences under certain circumstances provided by military laws. This can involve reducing, changing, or enhancing the punishment given by the court martial.
7. The Tribunal is considered a criminal court for certain specific provisions related to the penal code and criminal procedure, regardless of other provisions in this Act.

Definition and Interpretation of Arms Act, 1959

In this Act, the following definitions apply unless stated otherwise:

Acquisition: includes getting something by hiring, borrowing, or receiving it as a gift.
Ammunition: includes materials for firearms, such as rockets, bombs, grenades, and other projectiles, as well as items designed to hold or contain explosive or dangerous substances. This also covers charges for firearms, fuses, and machinery used to make ammunition.
Arms: refers to items used as weapons for offensive or defensive purposes, including firearms and deadly weapons. It doesn't cover items meant for domestic or agricultural use, like a stick or non-functional weapons for play.
District Magistrate: in areas with a Police Commissioner, refers to the Commissioner or Deputy with specified authority.
Firearms: any weapons designed to fire projectiles using explosives or energy, including artillery and devices that discharge harmful substances.
Licensing Authority: person or body authorized to grant or renew licenses under the Act.
Magistrate: an Executive Magistrate as per the Criminal Procedure Code 1973.
Prohibited Ammunition: refers to dangerous materials specified by the Central Government, including rockets, grenades, and articles for military purposes.
Prohibited Arms: weapons or firearms designed to continuously discharge projectiles or harmful substances. Includes artillery and arms designated as prohibited by the government.
Public Servant: as defined in the Indian Penal Code.
Transfer: includes activities like hiring, lending, giving, or handing over possession.

Additionally:

- The length of a firearm barrel is measured from the muzzle to where the charge explodes.
- References to laws not applicable in certain areas should be understood in relation to corresponding laws in force there.
- Mentions of officers or authorities without equivalents in an area should be interpreted based on designations specified by the Central Government.

In case of any discrepancies or additional requirements, the corresponding laws and authorities should be consulted.

Simplified text: Licensing of Firearms and Ammunition

Acquiring and Possessing Firearms and Ammunition:
No one can buy, own, or carry any firearms or ammunition unless they have a license issued according to the law and regulations. However, someone without a license can carry firearms or ammunition in the company of, or with written permission from, a licensed person for repair, renewal, or use by the licensed person.

Limit on Number of Firearms:
Except for certain individuals mentioned in another section, no one can have more than three firearms at any time. If someone already has more than three firearms when this law came into effect, they can keep three and must surrender the rest to the police station, a licensed dealer, or a military unit armory within ninety days.

Exceptions:
Certain exceptions exist for gun dealers, members of recognized rifle clubs or associations using specific types of rifles for target practice.

Further Provisions:
Certain rules regarding depositing extra firearms are laid out in section 21, similar to the rules for surrendering arms or ammunition.

Cancellation of License:
The authority to begin proceedings to cancel a license rests with the Additional District Magistrate (A.D.M.), as established in a court case.

Simplified text: Licensing for Arms in Specific Areas

The Arms Act of 1959 allows the Central Government to regulate the acquisition, possession, and carrying of certain types of arms in designated areas if it deems it necessary in the public interest. A notification in the Official Gazette can specify the areas to which this regulation applies. In those specified areas, individuals cannot acquire, possess, or carry arms of a specified class unless they hold a license issued under the Act and its accompanying rules.

Comments:
Lead used in industrial or manufacturing processes is not covered by this provision. However, if lead is in the form of a finished product like bullets or empty cartridges, it is considered 'ammunition.' Lead in the form of finished products like pencils is not included in this regulation.

Simplified text: Application for Licenses:
To get a license under Chapter II of the Arms Act, 1959, an application must be submitted to the licensing authority. The application should be in the required format, include necessary details, and be accompanied by the prescribed fee, if any.
Granting of Licenses:
Upon receiving an application, the licensing authority should request a report from the officer in charge of the nearest police station within the specified time. After conducting any necessary inquiries and reviewing the report, the licensing authority must, in writing, either approve or deny the license application as per the provisions of this Chapter.
Types of Licenses:
The licensing authority should issue a license under Section 3 for:
- Indian citizens requiring a smooth bore gun with a barrel of at least twenty inches for protection, sport, or muzzle loading guns for crop protection. In cases where a muzzle loading gun is deemed inadequate for crop protection, the authority may issue a license for another type of smooth bore gun for that purpose.
- Point 22 bore rifle or air rifle for target practice by a member of a licensed or recognized rifle club or association.
For any other cases or licenses under different sections, the licensing authority may grant a license if satisfied that the applicant has a valid reason for needing it.
Additional Comments:
- The licensing authority, which includes the Government, has the discretion to grant or deny a license even if all procedures have been followed.
- If an Indian citizen applies for a license for protection, the authority must issue it if the applicant meets the required conditions.
- While there is no specific time frame mentioned in the Act or Rules, if an application for a non-prohibited arm is not processed within three months, it will be considered approved. This is to prevent delays by the licensing authority in handling such applications.

Simplified text: Variation, Suspension, and Revocation of Licenses under the Arms Act, 1959

License Changes:
The authority that issues licenses can change the conditions of a license except for those that are already set. They can ask the license holder to return the license if needed.

Suspension or Revocation:
The authority can suspend a license for specific periods or revoke it if:
- The holder is prohibited by law from having arms or ammunition, is unfit mentally, or is deemed unsafe for holding a license.
- Suspending or revoking the license is necessary for public safety or peace.
- The license was obtained with incorrect or hidden information.
- The license conditions have been violated.
- The holder fails to return the license as requested.

The authority can also revoke a license upon the holder's request.

Recording and Furnishing Reasons:
If the authority makes any changes to a license or suspends/revokes it, they must provide written reasons and, upon request, a brief explanation to the license holder unless it's not in the public interest to do so.

Authority to Suspend or Revoke:
Any higher authority can also suspend or revoke licenses for the same reasons, following similar procedures.

Court Convictions:
A court convicting the license holder of an offense under the Arms Act or related rules can also suspend or revoke the license. If the conviction is overturned later, the suspension or revocation becomes void.

Central Government's Power:
The Central Government can issue orders to suspend or revoke licenses nationwide or in specific regions.

License Surrender:
If a license is suspended or revoked, the holder must promptly return it to the relevant authority as specified.

Simplified text: Offences and Penalties under the Arms Act, 1959
Manufacturing and Selling Arms:
Anyone who unlawfully makes, sells, transfers, handles, or has in their possession arms or ammunition that go against the law stated in section 5 will face imprisonment ranging from three to seven years and may also be fined.

Prohibited Arms Possession:
Anyone who acquires, has, or carries prohibited arms or ammunition against the law in section 7 could be sentenced to imprisonment from five to ten years and may also be fined. Moreover, those involved in manufacturing, selling, or having prohibited arms could face life imprisonment and fines.

Possession of Arms in Contravention:
Individuals unlawfully acquiring, having, or carrying firearms or ammunition against section 3 could be imprisoned for up to one year or fined.

Unauthorized Sale or Transfer:
Selling or transferring firearms, ammunition, or other arms without informing the authorities or before the prescribed period could result in imprisonment or fines.

License Violations:
Failure to surrender or deliver a license as requested by the licensing authority may lead to imprisonment or fines. Refusal to provide correct information when required may also result in penalties.

These simplified versions make the legal texts clearer and more understandable for the general public.

Using Arms Unlawfully: 
Using any type of weapons or ammunition against the rules in section 5 can lead to a prison sentence of at least three years and up to seven years, as well as a fine.
Using Prohibited Arms:

Format and details required for applying for a new license or renewing an existing one, and the deadline for renewal applications.

Criteria and conditions for granting, renewing, varying, suspending, or revoking licenses.

Duration for which a license remains valid when not specified by the Act.

Fees for license applications and renewals, as well as the method of payment.

Process for testing firearms.

Authorized firearms for training, age restrictions for users, and usage conditions.

Inspection rights for police or authorized government officers at premises where arms or ammunition are stored or manufactured.

Regulations for depositing arms or ammunition with licensed dealers or unit armorers, and conditions for potential forfeiture.

Any other matters that may need to be regulated.

Parliamentary Review:
Any rule established under this section must be presented to both houses of Parliament during a session and remain under review for thirty days. If both houses agree to modify or reject the rule within the following session(s), the rule will be implemented in the altered form or be revoked. Simplified text: Who is Covered by the Army Act, 1950
The Army Act applies to the following individuals, regardless of their location:
Regular Army officers, junior commissioned officers, and warrant officers.
Individuals enrolled under the Act.
Members of the Indian Reserve Forces.
Members of the Indian Supplementary Reserve Forces when called to service or during the annual test.
Officers of the Territorial Army when on duty, and enrolled personnel when called up or attached to regular forces, subject to any necessary changes under the Territorial Army Act, 1948.
Officers of the Indian Reserve of Officers and Indian Regular Reserve of Officers when performing duties they are liable for as reserve members.
Individuals not normally under military law who are on active service, in camp, on the march, or at specified frontier posts designated by the Central Government.
All individuals covered by clauses (a) to (g) remain subject to this Act until properly retired, discharged, released, removed, dismissed, or cashiered from service.

Simplified text: Definitions under the Army Act, 1950:

Active Service: When a person covered by this Act is involved in military operations against an enemy, in enemy-occupied territory, or part of a force occupying a foreign country.

Civil Offence: A crime that can be tried in a regular criminal court.

Civil Prison: A jail or detention facility used for criminal prisoners under the Prisons Act, 1894, or any current law.

Chief of the Army Staff: The officer in charge of the regular Army.

Commanding Officer: The officer responsible for specific sections of the regular Army or a department within it. They handle certain duties as specified in regulations or service customs.

Corps: A distinct group of individuals covered by this Act, designated as such for specific Act provisions.

Court-Martial: A military court convened according to this Act.

Criminal Court: A court that handles criminal cases in India.

Department: Includes divisions or branches within a department.

Enemy: Includes armed mutineers, rebels, rioters, pirates, or any armed individuals that necessitate action by those under military law.

Forces: Refers to the regular Army, Navy, and Air Force, or parts thereof.

Junior Commissioned Officer: An individual holding a junior officer rank in the regular Army or Indian Reserve Forces, subject to this Act.

Military Custody: Arrest or confinement according to military practices, including naval or air force custody.

Military Reward: Incentives such as gratuities, annuities, good conduct rewards, or pensions for service.

Non-Commissioned Officer: A person with a non-commissioned rank in the regular Army or Indian Reserve Forces, subject to this Act.

Notification: Official publication in the Gazette.

Offence: Any punishable act or omission under this Act, including civil offences.

Officer: A commissioned, gazetted, or paid officer in the regular Army or related forces, excluding certain ranks like junior commissioned officers, etc.

Prescribed: Set out in rules made under this Act.

Provost-Marshal: A person appointed under section 107 to maintain discipline, includes deputies, assistants, or those legally acting on their behalf.

Regular Army: Personnel like officers, non-commissioned officers, and others subject to duty anywhere worldwide.

Regulation: Rules established under this Act.

Superior Officer: Includes junior commissioned officers, warrant officers, non-commissioned officers, as well as officers of the Navy or Air Force.

Warrant Officer: A person appointed, gazetted, or paid as a warrant officer under this Act.

Undefined Terms: Terms not defined in this Act but explained in the Indian Penal Code shall have meanings as defined in that Code.

(1) Any person enrolled under this Act who is entitled under the conditions of his enrolment to be discharged, or whose discharge is ordered by competent authority, and who, when he is so entitled or ordered to be discharged, is serving out of India, and requests to be sent to India, shall, before being discharged, be sent to India with all convenient speed.

Section 26: Addressing Grievances (Army Act, 1950)
Grievances of Non-Officers:
Any individual under this Act who is not an officer, and feels unfairly treated by a superior or another officer, can take the following steps:
If not assigned to a specific unit, they can file a complaint with the officer in charge of their current command.
If part of a unit, they should address their complaint to the commanding officer of that unit.
If the officer being complained about is the one to whom the complaint should be made according to the above rules:
The aggrieved person can then escalate the complaint to the superior officer of the officer in question.
The officer who receives the complaint must thoroughly investigate the matter to provide proper redress to the complainant, or may escalate it further if necessary.

32. Priority in respect of army personnel's litigation.-
(1) On the presentation to any court by or on behalf of any person subject to this Act of a certificate from the proper military authority of leave of absence having been granted to or applied for by him for the purpose of prosecuting or defending any suit or other proceeding in such court, the court shall, on the application of such person, arrange, so far as may be possible, for the hearing and final disposal of such suit or other proceeding within the period of the leave so granted or applied for.

(3) No fee shall be payable to the court in respect of the presentation of any such certificate, or of any application by or on behalf of any such person, for priority for the hearing of his case.
(4) Where the court is unable to arrange for the hearing and final disposal of the suit or other proceeding within the period of such leave or intended leave as aforesaid, it shall record its reasons for its inability to do so, and shall cause a copy thereof to be furnished to such person on his application without any payment whatever by him in respect either of the application for such copy or of the copy itself.

When a person serving in the army needs to take legal action, they can present a certificate from the military confirming their leave to attend court proceedings. The court should make efforts to hear and resolve the case during the granted or applied-for leave period.

The military certificate should include the start and end dates of the leave, and details about the legal case.

No court fees apply for submitting the certificate or requesting priority for the case.

If the court can't resolve the case during the leave period, they must explain why and provide a free copy of the explanation to the person.

If there's any dispute about which military authority can issue the certificate, the matter will be referred to a high-ranking officer for a final decision.

SECTION 34 of Army Act, 1950
Chapter VI
Offences
34. Offences in relation to the enemy and punishable with death.-
Any person subject to this Act who commits any of the following offences, that is to say,-
(a) shamefully abandons or delivers up any garrison, fortress, post, place or guard, committed to his charge, or which it is his duty to defend, or uses any means to compel or induce any commanding officer or other person to commit any of the said acts; or
(b) intentionally uses any means to compel or induce any person subject to military, naval or air force law to abstain from acting against the enemy, or to discourage such person from acting against the enemy; or
(c) in the presence of the enemy, shamefully casts away his arms, ammunition, tools or equipment or misbehaves in such manner as to show cowardice; or
(d) treacherously holds correspondence with, or communicates intelligence to, the enemy or any person in arms against the Union; or
(e) directly or indirectly assists the enemy with money, arms, ammunition, stores or supplies; or
(f) treacherously or through cowardice sends a flag of truce to the enemy; or
(g) in time of war or during any military operation, intentionally occasions a false alarm in action, camp, garrison or quarters, or spreads reports calculated to create alarm or despondency; or
(h) in time of action leaves his commanding officer or his post, guard, picquet, patrol or party without being regularly relieved or without leave; or
(i) having been made a prisoner of war, voluntarily serves with or aids the enemy; or
(j) knowingly harbours or protects an enemy not being a prisoner; or
(k) being a sentry in time of war or alarm, sleeps upon his post or is intoxicated; or
(l) knowingly does any act calculated to imperil the success of the military, naval or air forces of India or any forces co-operating therewith or any part of such forces; shall, on conviction by court-martial, be liable to suffer death or such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned.
