SECTION 133 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 133     -    

Endorsement of certificate of registration on debenture or certificate of

debenture stock.
(1) The company shall cause a copy of every

certificate of registration given under section 132, to be endorsed on every

debenture or certificate of debenture stock which is issued by the company and

the payment of which is secured by the charge so registered :
Provided  that nothing in this sub-section shall

be construed as requiring a company to cause a certificate of registration of

any charge so given to be endorsed on any debenture or certificate of debenture

stock issued by the company before the charge was created.
(2) If any person knowingly delivers, or willfully

authorizes or permits the delivery of, any debenture or certificate of

debenture stock which, under the provisions of sub-section (1), is required to

have endorsed on it a copy of a certificate of registration without the copy

being so endorsed upon it, he shall, without prejudice to any other liability,

be punishable with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Debentures and Stock Certificates:

Certificate Endorsement: The company must include a copy of the registration certificate on every debenture or stock certificate issued by the company, securing payment with the registered charge. However, this is not required for debentures issued before the charge was created.

Non-Endorsement Penalty: Anyone knowingly delivering a debenture without the required endorsement may face a fine up to ten thousand rupees, in addition to any other legal consequences.

legal_text:
SECTION 137 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 137    -     Entry

in register of charges of appointment of receiver or manager. 
(1) If any person obtains an order for the

appointment of a receiver of, or of a person to manage, the property of a

company, or if any person appoints such receiver or person under any powers

contained in any instrument, he shall, within thirty days from the date of the

passing of the order or of the making of the appointment under the said powers,

give notice of the fact to the Registrar ; and the Registrar shall, on payment

of the prescribed fee, enter the fact in the register of charges.
(2) Where any person so appointed under the

powers contained in any instrument ceases to act as such, he shall, on so

ceasing, give to the Registrar notice to that effect ; and the Registrar shall

enter the notice in the register of charges.
(3) If any person makes default in complying

with the requirements of sub-section (1) or (2), he shall be punishable with

fine which may extend to five hundred rupees for every day during which the

default continues.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Registering Receiver or Manager Appointment:
- If someone is appointed as a receiver or manager for a company's property by court order or under a legal document, they must inform the Registrar within 30 days.
- The Registrar will add this information to the register of charges after the appropriate fee is paid.
- When the appointed person stops working in that role, they must also inform the Registrar.
Penalty for Non-compliance:
- Failure to adhere to these requirements may result in a fine of up to five hundred rupees per day for each day of non-compliance.

SECTION 138 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 138    -    

Company to report satisfaction and procedure thereafter. 
(1) The company shall give intimation to the

Registrar of the payment or satisfaction, in full, of any charge relating to

the company and requiring registration under this Part, within thirty days from

the date of such payment or satisfaction.
(2) The Registrar shall, on receipt of such

intimation, cause a notice to be sent to the holder of the charge calling upon

him to show cause within a time (not exceeding fourteen days) specified in such

notice, why payment or satisfaction should not be recorded as intimated to the

Registrar.
(3) If no cause is shown, the Registrar shall

order that a memorandum of satisfaction shall be entered in the register of

charges.
(4) If cause is shown, the Registrar shall

record a note to that effect in the register, and shall inform the company that

he has done so.
(5) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to

affect the power of the Registrar to make an entry in the register of charges

under section 139 otherwise than on receipt of an intimation from the company
simplified_text:
Simplified text: COMPANY CHARGE
Reporting Payment: The company must inform the Registrar within 30 days when a charge related to the company is fully paid off.
Registrar's Notice: The Registrar will notify the charge holder, giving them 14 days to object to the payment being marked as satisfied.
Recording Satisfaction: If no objections are raised, the Registrar will note the charge as satisfied in the register.
Objections Noted: If objections are raised, the Registrar will make a note of it and inform the company.
Registrar's Authority: The Registrar can still make entries in the register of charges even without receiving notification from the company.

SECTION 141 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 141    -    

Rectification by Company Law Board of register of charges. 
(1) The Company Law Board, on being satisfied
(a) that the omission to file with the

Registrar the particulars of any charge created by a company or of any charge

subject to which any property has been acquired by the company or of any

modification of any such charge or of any issue of debentures of a series, or

that the omission to register any charge within the time required by this Part,

or that the omission to give intimation to the Registrar of the payment or

satisfaction of a charge, within the time required by this Part, or that the

omission or mis-statement of any particular with respect to any such charge,

modification or issue of debentures of a series or with respect to any

memorandum of satisfaction or other entry made in pursuance of sections 138 and

139, was accidental or due to inadvertence or to some other sufficient cause or

is not of a nature to prejudice the position of creditors or shareholders of

the company ; or
(b) that on other grounds it is just and

equitable to grant relief ;
may, on the application of the company or any

person interested and on such terms and conditions as seem to the Company Law

Board just and expedient, direct that the time for the filing of the

particulars or for the registration of the charge or for the giving of intimation

of payment or satisfaction shall be extended or, as the case may require, that

the omission or mis-statement shall be rectified.
(2) The Company Law Board may make such order

as to the costs of an application under sub-section (1) as it thinks fit.
(3) Where the Company Law Board extends the

time for the registration of a charge, the order shall not prejudice any rights

acquired in respect of the property concerned before the charge is actually

registered.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Rectification of Charge Records:
If the Company Law Board finds that:
a) a company failed to provide details of a charge created, modified, or registered on time, or failed to inform the Registrar about the payment or satisfaction of a charge, and this was due to an unintentional error or a valid reason that doesn't harm the creditors or shareholders; or
b) it is fair and reasonable to rectify the situation for other reasons;
the Board can extend the time for filing or registering the charge, or correct any mistakes or omissions. This can be done upon a request from the company or any interested party, with conditions set by the Board.
The Board can also decide on the costs related to such applications. If the Board extends the time for charge registration, it will not affect any rights established concerning the property before the charge is officially registered.

legal_text:
SECTION 142 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 142    -    

Penalties. 
(1) If default is made in filing with the

Registrar for registration the particulars
(a) of any charge created by the company ;
(b) of the payment or satisfaction of a debt

in respect of which a charge has been registered under this Part ; or
(c) of the issues of debentures of a series ;
requiring registration with the Registrar

under the provisions of this Part, then, unless the registration has been

effected on the application of some other person, the company, and every

officer of the company or other person who is in default, shall be punishable

with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees for every day during which

the default continues.
(2) Subject as aforesaid, if any company makes

default in complying with any of the other requirements of this Act as to the

registration with the Registrar of any charge created by the company or of any

fact connected therewith, the company, and every officer of the company who is

in default, shall, without prejudice to any other liability, be punishable with

fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Penalties for Not Registering Charges

Failing to Register Charges:
If a company doesn't register details of a charge it created, or the payment of a debt related to a charge, or the issue of a series of debentures, as required by law, the company, its officers, or anyone else at fault may be fined up to five thousand rupees per day until the registration is done.

Other Registration Defaults:
Apart from the above, if a company fails to comply with any other registration requirements regarding charges under the Companies Act, the company and its officers may face a fine of up to ten thousand rupees, in addition to any other consequences.

SECTION 144 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 144    -     Right

to inspect copies of instruments creating charges and company's register of

charges. 
(1) The copies of instruments creating charges

kept in pursuance of section 136, and the register of charges kept in pursuance

of section 143, shall be open during business hours (but subject to such

reasonable restrictions as the company in general meeting may impose, so that

not less than two hours in each day are allowed for inspection) to the

inspection of any creditor or member of the company without fee, at the

registered office of the company.
(2) The register of charges kept in pursuance

of section 143 shall also be open, during business hours but subject to the

reasonable restrictions aforesaid, to the inspection of any other person on

payment of a fee of such sum as may be prescribed for each inspection, at the

registered office of the company.
(3) If the inspection of the said copies or

register is refused, the company, and every officer of the company who is in

default, shall be punishable with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees

and with a further fine which may extend to two hundred rupees for every day

during which the refusal continues.
(4) The Company Law Board may also by order

compel an immediate inspection of the said copies or register.

- Creditors and members of the company can access copies of loan documents and the company's record of loans at the company's registered office during business hours. 
- Other individuals can access the record of loans by paying a prescribed fee for each inspection.

SECTION 145 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 145    -    

Application of Part to charges requiring registration under it but not under

previous law. 
In respect of any charge created before, and remaining

unsatisfied at, the commencement of this Act, which, if this Act had been in

force at the relevant time, would have had to be registered by the company in

pursuance of this Part but which did not require registration under the Indian

Companies Act, 1913 (7 of 1913), and in respect of all matters relating to such

charge, the provisions of this Part shall apply and have effect in all

respects, as if the date of commencement of this Act had been substituted

therein for the date of creation of the charge, or the date of completion of

the acquisition of the property subject to the charge as the case may be.

Nothing contained in this section shall be deemed to affect the relative

priorities as they existed immediately before the commencement of this Act, as

between charges on the same property.

SECTION 146 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 146    -    

Registered office of company.
(1) A company shall, as from the day on which

it begins to carry on business, or as from the thirtieth day after the date of

its incorporation whichever is earlier, have a registered office to which all

communications and notices may be addressed.
(2) Notice of the situation of the registered

office, and of every change therein, shall be given within thirty days after

the date of the incorporation of the company or after the date of the change,

as the case may be, to the Registrar who shall record the same :
Provided  that except on the authority of a

special resolution passed by the company, the registered office of the company

shall not be removed
(a) in the case of an existing company,

outside the local limits of any city, town or village where such office is situated

at the commencement of this Act, or where it may be situated later by virtue of

a special resolution passed by the company ; and
(b) in the case of any other company, outside

the local limits of any city, town or village where such office is first situated,

or where it may be situated later by virtue of a special resolution passed by

the company.
(3) The inclusion in the annual return of a

company of a statement as to the address of its registered office shall not be

taken to satisfy the obligation imposed by sub-section (2).
(4) If default is made in complying with the

requirements of this section, the company, and, every officer of the company

who is in default, shall be punishable with fine which may extend to five

hundred rupees for every day during which the default continues.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Registered Office:
- A company must have a registered office where all communications and notices can be sent, starting from the day it begins operating or the thirtieth day after its incorporation, whichever is earlier.
- Any change in the location of the registered office must be notified to the Registrar within thirty days of incorporation or the change, and the Registrar must update the records.
- The registered office cannot be moved without a special resolution passed by the company, and in certain cases, it cannot be moved outside specific local limits without approval.
- Including the registered office address in the annual return does not fulfill the requirement of notifying the Registrar of any change in the location.
- Failure to comply with these requirements can result in a fine of up to five hundred rupees per day of non-compliance for both the company and any officer involved.

SECTION 147 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 147    -    

Publication of name by company. 
(1) Every company
(a) shall paint or affix its name and the

address of its registered office, and keep the same painted or affixed, on the

outside of every office or place in which its business is carried on, in a

conspicuous position, in letters easily legible ; and if the characters

employed therefore are not those of the language, or of one of the languages,

in general use in that locality, also in the characters of that language or of

one of those languages ;
(b) shall have its name engraven in legible

characters on its seal ; and
(c) shall have its name and the address of its

registered office mentioned in legible characters in all its business letters,

in all its bill heads and letter paper, and in all its notices and other

official publications ; and also have its name so mentioned in all bills of

exchange, hundis, promissory notes, endorsements, cheques and orders for money

or goods purporting to be signed by or on behalf of the company, and in all

bills of parcels, invoices, receipts and letters of credit of the company.
(2) If a company does not paint or affix its

name and the address of its registered office, or keep the same painted or

affixed in the manner directed by clause (a) of sub-section (1), the company,

and every officer of the company who is in default, shall be punishable with

fine which may extend to five hundred rupees for not so painting or affixing

its name and the address of its registered office, and for every day during

which its name and the address of its registered office, is not so kept painted

or affixed.
(3) If a company fails to comply with clause

(b) or clause (c) of sub-section (1), the company shall be punishable with fine

which may extend to five thousand rupees.
(4) If an officer of a company or any person

on its behalf
(a) uses, or authorizes the use of, any seal

purporting to be a seal of the company whereon its name is not engraven in the

manner aforesaid ;
(b) issues, or authorizes the issue of, any

business letter, bill head, letter paper, notice or other official publication

of the company wherein its name and the address of its registered office are

not mentioned in the manner aforesaid ;
(c) signs, or authorizes to be signed, on behalf

of the company, any bill of exchange, hundi, promissory note, endorsement,

cheque or order for money or goods where in its name is not mentioned in the

manner aforesaid; or
(d) issues, or authorizes the issue of, any

bill of parcels, invoice, receipt or letter of credit of the company, wherein

its name is not mentioned in the manner aforesaid ;
such officer or person shall be punishable

with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, and shall further be

personally liable to the holder of the bill of exchange, hundi, promissory

note, cheque or order for money or goods, for the amount thereof, unless it is

duly paid by the company.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Naming and Address Requirements for Companies

Required Display:
1. Every company must prominently display its name and registered office address outside all locations where it operates, using easily readable letters.
2. The company's name must also be clearly engraved on its official seal.
3. The company's name and registered office address must be included in all business correspondence, such as letters, bills, and notices, using legible characters.
Consequences of Non-Compliance:
1. Failure to display the name and address outside business premises may result in a fine of up to five hundred rupees per day.
2. Not following the engraving and display requirements for the seal or business correspondence may lead to a fine of up to five thousand rupees.
Penalties for Officers:
1. Company officers or authorized persons using seals or issuing documents without the required name and address may face fines of up to five thousand rupees and personal liability for any outstanding payments unless settled by the company.

legal_text:
SECTION 149 of Companies Act, 1956
Companies Act, 1956
Sec 149    -    

Restrictions on commencement of business. 
(1) Where a company having a share capital has

issued a prospectus inviting the public to subscribe for its shares, the

company shall not commence any business or exercise any borrowing powers,

unless
(a) shares held subject to the payment of the

whole amount thereof in cash have been allotted to an amount not less in the

whole than the minimum subscription ;
(b) every director of the company has paid to

the company, on each of the shares taken or contracted to be taken by him and

for which he is liable to pay in cash, a proportion equal to the proportion

payable on application and allotment on the shares offered for public

subscription ;
(c) no money is, or may become, liable to be

repaid to applicants for any shares or debentures which have been offered for

public subscription by reason of any failure to apply for, or to obtain,

permission for the shares or debentures to be dealt in on any recognized stock

exchange ; and
(d) there has been filed with the Registrar a

duly verified declaration by one of the directors or the secretary or, where

the company has not appointed a secretary, a secretary in whole-time practice,

in the prescribed form, that clauses (a), (b) and (c) of this sub-section, have

been complied with.
(2) Where a company having a share capital has

not issued a prospectus inviting the public to subscribe for its shares, the

company shall not commence any business or exercise any borrowing powers,

unless
(a) there has been filed with the Registrar a

statement in lieu of the prospectus ;
(b) every director of the company has paid to

the company, on each of the shares taken or contracted to be taken by him and

for which he is liable to pay in cash, a proportion equal to the proportion

payable on application and allotment on the shares payable in cash ; and
(c) there has been filed with Registrar a duly

verified declaration by one of the directors or the secretary or, where the

company has not appointed a secretary, a secretary in whole-time practice, in

the prescribed form, that clause (b) of this sub-section has been complied with.
(2A) Without prejudice to the provisions of

sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) a company having a share capital, whether

or not it has issued a prospectus inviting the public to subscribe for its

shares, shall not at any time commence any business
(a) if such company is a company in existence

has been complied with ;

in contravention of this sub-section, every person who is responsible for the

with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees for every day during which

the contravention continues.

and that certificate shall be conclusive evidence that the company is so

entitled.

liability, be punishable with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees for

every day during which the contravention continues.

Restrictions on Starting Business for Companies:
1. If a company with shares has issued a prospectus to the public and wants to start business or borrow money, certain conditions must be met:
   - Ensure that shares have been allotted with the full payment required in cash.
   - Every director must pay a specified amount for the shares they own in cash.
   - No repayment should occur to applicants due to stock exchange issues.
   - File a verified declaration with the Registrar proving compliance with these conditions.

2. If a company with shares has not issued a prospectus to the public and wants to start business or borrow money, the following rules apply:
   - File a statement with the Registrar instead of a prospectus.
   - Every director must pay a specific proportion for their shares in cash.
   - File a verified declaration showing compliance with the share payment condition.

3. No company with shares can start a new business if its objects in the memorandum relate to specific matters. Approval by a special resolution in a general meeting and a verified declaration are necessary.

4. A company cannot start a business not relevant to its current operations unless a special resolution is passed, or Central Government approval is obtained based on member votes.

5. The Registrar certifies a company's entitlement to start business after receiving the necessary declarations or statements.

6. Contracts made before the company is allowed to start business are provisional until that date.

7. This section does not apply to private companies or those registered before April 1, 1914, without a public prospectus.

shall, within fourteen days after the date on which any alteration is made in

Definitions:
1. Abridged Prospectus: A short document with key features of a prospectus, as specified by the Securities and Exchange Board.
2. Accounting Standards: Standards for accounting specified for companies under section 133.

6. Associate Company: A company in which another company has significant influence, with "significant influence" defined as control of at least twenty percent of share capital or business decisions.
7. Auditing Standards: Standards for auditing companies under section 143.
8. Authorized Capital: Maximum share capital permitted by a company's memorandum.
9. Banking Company: Defined as per the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
10. Board of Directors: The collective directors of a company.
11. Body Corporate: Includes companies incorporated outside India, excluding co-operative societies.
12. Book and Paper: Includes various documents like account books, deeds, minutes kept in paper or electronic form.
13. Books of Account: Records of money transactions, sales, assets, and liabilities, including prescribed cost items.
14. Branch Office: An establishment described as such by a company.
15. Called-up Capital: Capital called for payment.
16. Charge: An interest or lien created on a company's assets as security.
17. Chartered Accountant: Defined as per the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.
18. Chief Executive Officer: Officer designated as such by a company.
19. Chief Financial Officer: Person appointed as the CFO of a company.
20. Company: A company incorporated under the Act or previous laws.
21. Company Limited by Guarantee: Liability limited to members' contributions.
22. Company Limited by Shares: Liability limited to unpaid share amounts.
23. Company Liquidator: Person appointed for winding up a company.
24. Company Secretary: Official appointed to perform specific functions under the Act.
25. Company Secretary in Practice: A practicing company secretary.
26. Contributory: Person liable to contribute to company assets in case of winding up.
27. Control: Includes right to appoint directors or influence management decisions.
28. Cost Accountant: Defined as per the Cost and Works Accountants Act, 1959.

Memorandum:
1. The company's memorandum must include:
   a. The company's name, ending with "Limited" for a public limited company or "Private Limited" for a private limited company, except for companies registered under section 8.
   b. The location of the company's registered office.
   c. The company's purpose and any other necessary details.
   d. The members' liability, whether limited or unlimited, including:
      i. For a company limited by shares, members' liability is limited to any unpaid amounts on their shares.
      ii. For a company limited by guarantee, each member's commitment to contribute to the company's assets in case of winding up.

   e. For companies with share capital:
      i. The total share capital and its division into fixed amount shares.
      ii. The number of shares each subscriber intends to subscribe, with a minimum of one share.

   f. For One Person Companies, the designated successor in case of the subscriber's demise.

2. The company's name in the memorandum must not:
   a. Be identical or similar to existing company names or against the law.
   b. Contain words implying government affiliation without approval.

3. The company's name should not suggest connections with governments, authorities, or bodies without approval.

4. An application can be made to the Registrar for reserving or changing a company name.

When some members of a company, along with the Board of Directors, want to sell some or all of their shares to the public, they can do so following the rules laid down by the law.

Simplified text: Civil Liability for Misleading Statements in Prospectus

If a person buys company securities based on misleading information in the prospectus and suffers losses as a result, the company and certain individuals will be responsible for compensating the person. These individuals include:

- Directors of the company when the prospectus was issued.
- Individuals who allowed their names to be used as directors in the prospectus.
- Promoters of the company.
- Individuals who authorized the prospectus.
- Experts mentioned in section 26(5).

These individuals will have to pay compensation for any losses suffered by the person. However, a person will not be liable if they can prove that they:
- Withdrew their consent to be a director before the prospectus was issued without their knowledge.
- Were unaware of or did not consent to the prospectus and immediately made a public notice once they became aware.

If it is proven that the prospectus was issued with fraudulent intent, all the individuals mentioned earlier will be personally responsible for any losses incurred by investors, without any limit on liability.

Simplified text: 
Reducing Share Capital:

A company with share capital can reduce its share capital by special resolution, subject to approval by the Tribunal. This may involve: 
- Cancelling or reducing liability on unpaid shares
- Adjusting paid-up share capital to match the company's needs, either by canceling excess capital or paying it off

Approval Process:
- The Tribunal must notify the Central Government, Registrar, market authority (for listed companies), and creditors about the application for reduction.
- If no objections are received within three months, it is presumed that there are no issues.

Confirmation and Publication:
- The Tribunal can approve the reduction if all creditors' claims are secured or settled, following accounting standards.
- The Tribunal's confirmation order must be published as directed.

Registration:
- The company must provide a certified copy of the Tribunal's order and a minute detailing the reduced capital to the Registrar within 30 days.
- The Registrar will register the details and issue a certificate.

Liabilities:
- Members are not liable for more than the difference between the paid amount on their shares and the reduced amount after the reduction.
- If a creditor is not listed and cannot be paid post-reduction, members at the time of registration may be called upon to contribute.

Officer Responsibilities:
- Any officer knowingly concealing or misrepresenting creditor information may be held liable under the law.

Penalties:
- Failure to comply with the registration requirement may result in fines ranging from five lakh rupees to twenty-five lakh rupees.

Simplified text: Power to Buy Back Securities

1. A company can buy back its own shares or specified securities using:
  a. Free reserves,
  b. Securities premium account, or
  c. Proceeds from the issue of shares or securities.
  - The company cannot buy back shares using funds from an earlier share issue of the same kind.

2. Conditions for buy-back:
  - Authorized by the company's articles.
  - Special resolution passed at a general meeting.
    - Exception: No need for a special resolution if the buy-back is 10% or less of the total equity capital and free reserves, and approved by the Board via a resolution.
    - The buy-back should not exceed 25% of the paid-up capital and free reserves. This percentage may vary based on the total paid-up equity capital for the financial year.
    - The ratio of debts after buy-back should not be more than twice the paid-up capital and free reserves. The government may set different ratios for different types of companies.
    - All shares bought back should be fully paid-up.
    - Buy-back of listed securities should follow the regulations of the Securities and Exchange Board.
    - Buy-back of other securities should comply with prescribed rules.
    - No buy-back offer should be made within a year after a previous buy-back offer.

3. Information to be provided:
  - Full disclosure of material facts.
  - Reasons for buy-back.
  - Type of shares or securities to be bought back.
  - Amount to be invested.
  - Timeline for completing the buy-back.

4. Buy-back completion:
  - Buy-back must be completed within one year from passing the resolution.

5. Methods of buy-back:
  - Proportionate buy-back from existing shareholders or security holders.
  - Purchase from the open market.
  - Buying securities issued to employees under stock option or sweat equity schemes.

6. Before buy-back:
  - Company must file a solvency declaration with the Registrar and Securities and Exchange Board, signed by two directors verifying the company's solvency for at least a year.
  - Unlisted companies need not file with the Securities and Exchange Board.

7. Post buy-back:
  - Bought back shares or securities must be destroyed within seven days.
  - Company cannot issue the same kind of shares or securities for six months post buy-back, except for specific purposes as outlined.

8. Register maintenance:
  - Maintain a register of bought-back shares or securities with necessary details.

9. Return filing:
  - File a return with Registrar and Securities and Exchange Board within 30 days of completing the buy-back.

10. Penalty for non-compliance:
  - Non-compliance with regulations may result in a fine of ₹1 - ₹3 lakh for the company.
  - Officers in default may face imprisonment up to three years or a fine of ₹1 - ₹3 lakh, or both.

Explanation:
- "Specified securities" include employees’ stock options or other securities notified by the Central Government.
- "Free reserves" encompass the securities premium account.

Simplified text: Duty to Register Charges:

Every company, whether in India or outside, must register any charge they create on their property, assets, or any tasks they undertake, within 30 days of creating it. This registration includes providing details of the charge signed by the company and the charge-holder, along with any related documents, paying required fees, and following the prescribed process. In certain cases, the registration can be allowed within 300 days upon an application and payment of additional fees.

Extension of Time: If registration is not completed within 300 days, the company must request an extension under section 87. Any delay in registration does not affect rights acquired regarding the property before registration.

Certificate of Registration: Upon registering a charge, the Registrar issues a certificate to the company and the charge-holder.

Validity of Registered Charges: A charge must be registered to be considered valid by the liquidator or any creditor. Any charge not registered is not recognized unless duly registered and certified by the Registrar.

Protection of Contracts: The requirement of registration does not impact any existing contracts or obligations related to the repayment of money secured by a charge.

Reporting Satisfaction of Charge:
A company must inform the Registrar using the required form when a charge registered under this Chapter is fully paid or satisfied. This notification must be made within 30 days from the date of payment or satisfaction. Similar to Section 77(1), the rules apply to this notification.

2. The notice for a meeting of a company with share capital or with provisions for proxy voting must prominently state that a member can appoint a proxy to vote on their behalf, and the proxy does not need to be a member.

3. Any officer of the company who fails to comply with the above rule shall be fined up to five thousand rupees.

4. If the articles of a company require proxies to be appointed more than 48 hours before a meeting, the 48-hour rule will apply for the validity of proxy appointments.

5. Any officer who, at the expense of the company, sends out proxy appointment invitations to members shall be fined up to one lakh rupees if they do so knowingly without proper authorization.

The appointment of a proxy must:

6. Be in writing and signed by the appointer or an authorized attorney, or sealed if the appointer is a corporation.

7. If a prescribed form is used, any proxy instrument must not be questioned based on specific requirements in the company's articles.

Every member entitled to vote at a meeting can inspect the proxies lodged with the company during business hours, provided they give three days' notice in writing.

Voluntary Revision of Financial Statements or Board’s Report

If the directors of a company believe that either:
a. The company's financial statement, or
b. The Board's report, does not follow the rules in section 129 or section 134, they can create a new financial statement or report for any of the last three financial years. a. Correcting issues that violated sections 129 or 134, and
b. Making any necessary changes that result from the corrections.

a. Replace or supplement the previous financial statement or report with a document showing the needed corrections,
b. Define the auditor's role concerning the revised financial statement or report, and
c. Instruct the directors on what actions they need to take as required.

Simplified text: Establishment of National Financial Reporting Authority
1.  Creation of Authority: The Government may establish a National Financial Reporting Authority to handle matters related to accounting and auditing standards under this Act.
2. Duties of the Authority:
    a. Advising Government: Providing recommendations to the Government on setting accounting and auditing policies for adoption by companies or auditors.
    b. Monitoring Compliance: Ensuring that companies and auditors follow accounting and auditing standards as required.
    c. Oversight: Supervising the quality of services provided by professionals who help ensure compliance with standards and suggesting ways to improve service quality.
 3. Authority Structure: The Authority will consist of a chairperson, who must be well-qualified in areas like accountancy, auditing, finance, or law, and up to fifteen members, including both part-time and full-time members.
 4. Investigative Powers:
    a. Initiating Investigations: The Authority can investigate on its own or based on a reference from the Government regarding professional misconduct by chartered accountants or firms.
    b. Enforcement Powers: Holding powers similar to a civil court, such as accessing documents, examining individuals under oath, inspecting records, and issuing commissions for obtaining evidence.
    c. Imposing Penalties: The Authority can penalize individuals or firms found guilty of misconduct, including fines and banning from practicing for a specific period.
 5. Appeal Process: Individuals dissatisfied with a decision of the Authority may appeal to an Appellate Authority set up by the Government.
 6. Additional Provisions:
    a. Appointment of Appellate Authority: The Government can form an Appellate Authority to hear appeals against decisions of the Financial Reporting Authority.
    b. Operational Details: The selection process, terms of office, support staff requirements, and appeal filing procedures for the Appellate Authority will be specified.
    c. Annual Reporting: The Authority must submit an annual report of its activities to the Government, which will be presented to Parliament.
    d. Administration: The Authority can appoint a secretary and other staff as needed, with their terms and conditions determined by regulations.
    e. Accountability: The Authority's accounts will be audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, with reports provided to the Government and Parliament annually.

1. Approval of Financial Statements: The Board of Directors must approve the financial statements, including any consolidated statements, before they are signed. This should be done by the chairperson, two directors (including the managing director if applicable), the Chief Executive Officer (if a director), the Chief Financial Officer, and the company secretary.

   - Corporate social responsibility initiatives
   - Evaluation of Board performance
   - Any other prescribed matters

4. Directors' Responsibility Statement: This statement should confirm adherence to accounting standards, consistent application of policies, maintenance of accounting records, going concern basis, internal financial controls, compliance with laws, and effective compliance systems.

Simplified text: Appointment of Auditors:
Every company must appoint an individual or firm as an auditor at its first annual general meeting. The auditor will serve from the end of that meeting until the conclusion of the sixth annual general meeting and every sixth meeting after that. Procedures for selecting auditors at these meetings will be as prescribed.

Auditor Services:
Auditors must consent to their appointment and provide certification that they meet the necessary conditions. The company must inform the appointed auditor and file a notice with the Registrar within 15 days of the appointment.

Listed companies or prescribed company classes cannot appoint the same individual auditor for more than five consecutive years, or the same audit firm for more than two consecutive terms of five years. Government Company Auditors:
For government-owned or controlled companies, the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India must appoint a qualified auditor within 180 days of the financial year's start. The first auditor of a non-government company should be appointed by the Board of Directors within 30 days of registration.

Audit Committee and Appointments:
If an Audit Committee is mandatory under section 177, all auditor appointments, including filling casual vacancies, must be made considering the committee's recommendations. If no auditor is appointed or re-appointed at an annual general meeting, the existing auditor will continue in that role.

Simplified text: Auditor's Rights and Duties:

Access and Information: An auditor has the right to access a company's financial records and vouchers, regardless of where they are kept. They can also request information and explanations from company officers as needed to perform their duties.

Inquiry Areas: The auditor must review various matters, including the security of loans and advances made by the company, the impact of certain transactions on the company's interests, and whether company assets like shares have been sold at appropriate prices.

Reporting: The auditor is required to report to the company's members on the accounts and financial statements examined. The report should confirm if the financial statements provide a true and fair view of the company's financial status, among other things.

Additional Disclosures: The auditor's report should include details on information gathering, adequacy of company records, compliance with accounting standards, internal financial controls, and other pertinent matters. If any concerns or qualifications exist, these must be stated with reasons.

Government Company Audit: In the case of a government company, the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India appoints and supervises auditors for the company. The audit report must be submitted to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, and any comments provided must be shared with relevant stakeholders.

Auditing Standards: Auditors must adhere to specified auditing standards. The Central Government may prescribe these standards in consultation with the relevant authorities and can direct specific additional disclosures in the auditor's report for certain types of companies.

Fraud Reporting: If an auditor suspects fraudulent activities within the company, they must promptly report it to the Central Government as prescribed.

Compliance Enforcement: Non-compliance with reporting requirements can result in fines for auditors, cost accountants, or company secretaries in practice.

Simplified text: Audit of Cost Records for Certain Companies

Government Order: The Central Government can instruct certain companies, based on the goods they produce or services they offer, to include details about material usage, labor, or other costs in their accounting records. Before issuing the order for companies regulated under a special Act, consultation with the relevant regulatory body is required.

Cost Audit: If deemed necessary, the Central Government can mandate that companies meeting specific financial criteria conduct a cost record audit, which will be carried out by a Cost Accountant appointed by the company's Board. The appointed auditor must adhere to cost auditing standards set by the Institute of Cost and Works Accountants of India, approved by the Central Government.

Additional Audit: The cost audit under this section is separate from the regular audit required under section 143 of the Companies Act.

Responsibilities: The qualifications, disqualifications, rights, duties, and obligations applicable to auditors under the Companies Act also apply to cost auditors. The company must cooperate with the cost auditor and ensure that the audit report is submitted to the Board of Directors.

Reporting: The company must provide a copy of the cost audit report to the Central Government within thirty days of receipt, along with explanations for any reservations or qualifications. Upon reviewing the report, if additional information is needed, the Government can request it from the company.

Non-compliance: Failure to comply with these provisions can result in penalties for the company, its officers, and the cost auditor as specified in the Act.

1. Board Responsibility: The board of directors of listed companies and other specified companies must establish a Nomination and Remuneration Committee. This committee should consist of at least three non-executive directors, with at least half of them being independent.

Simplified text: Powers of Board of Directors under Companies Act, 2013

The Board of Directors of a company has the authority to exercise all powers and perform all necessary actions specified for the company. However, these powers must be exercised in compliance with the regulations set forth in the Companies Act, the company's memorandum or articles, and any consistent regulations established, including those decided by the company in a general meeting.

The Board cannot undertake any action that should be performed by the company in a general meeting, according to the Act, the company's memorandum, articles, or any other relevant regulations.

The Board is empowered to make decisions regarding the following matters through resolutions passed during Board meetings:

- Collecting unpaid money from shareholders on their shares
- Authorizing securities buy-back as per Section 68
- Issuing securities, such as debentures, within or outside India
- Borrowing money
- Investing the company's funds
- Granting loans, guarantees, or security for loans
- Approving financial statements and the Board's report
- Diversifying the company's business
- Approving amalgamation, merger, or reconstruction
- Acquiring or taking over another company or a significant stake in it
- Any other matters as may be prescribed

The Board has the option to delegate specific powers to committees, managing directors, managers, or other key officers of the company through a resolution passed during a meeting, subject to specified conditions.

Notably, standard banking activities, such as accepting deposits or placing monies on deposit, are not considered as borrowing or lending under this section when carried out by a banking company.

This section does not limit the company's ability to place restrictions and conditions on the exercise of powers by the Board during a general meeting.

- Companies are generally not allowed to give loans, guarantees, or securities to their directors or any other person linked to the director, except in specific cases mentioned below.
2. Permissible Scenarios

- If a company violates the lending restrictions, it may face a fine ranging from five lakh rupees to twenty-five lakh rupees.

SECTION 186 of Companies Act, 2013 - Loan and Investment

1. Company Investment:
- A company can invest through at most two layers of investment companies.
- Exceptions: 
  - Acquiring a foreign company with more than two layers of subsidiaries, as permitted by that country's laws.
  - Subsidiary companies can have investment subsidiaries to meet legal requirements.

2. Loan and Investment Restrictions:
- Companies cannot:
  - Give loans to individuals or other corporations.
  - Offer guarantees or provide security for loans to other entities.
  - Acquire securities of another company beyond specified limits.

3. Approval Requirements:
- Special resolution approval at a general meeting is necessary for any loan, guarantee, security, or acquisitions exceeding the limits.

4. Disclosure:
- Companies must fully disclose loans, investments, guarantees, or security details in financial statements.

5. Approval Process:
- Board consent, approval of public financial institution for existing term loans, and no defaults are prerequisites for new investments or loans.

6. Additional Regulations:
- Companies regulated by SEBI Act, 1992 have limits on inter-corporate loans/deposits.
- Loans must have interest rates based on prevailing government security yields.
- Defaulting companies cannot give loans, guarantees, or securities.

7. Record Keeping:
- Companies must maintain a register with prescribed details at their registered office.
- Members can inspect the register with payment of prescribed fees.

8. Exemptions:
- Certain entities like banks, insurance companies, or those in the securities business have exceptions.
- Non-banking financial companies have specific exemptions related to investments and lending.

9. Penalty:
- Violation of regulations leads to fines and possible imprisonment for officers in default.

10. Rule-making Authority:
- Central Government can create rules for the effective implementation of this section.

Explanation:
- Investment company: A company focused on acquiring shares, debentures, or securities.
- Infrastructure facilities: Facilities specified in Schedule VI.

Simplified text: Related Party Transactions

In the Companies Act, 2013, Section 188 focuses on transactions with related parties within a company. Here are the key points simplified:

Consent: A company needs the approval of its Board of Directors, given through a resolution at a board meeting, before entering into any contract or arrangement with a related party. This applies to various activities like sales, purchases, leases, appointments, and underwriting securities.

Special Approval: For certain transactions above a prescribed amount or limit, the company must seek special approval through a shareholders' special resolution. Members who are related parties cannot vote on such resolutions.

Exceptions: Transactions made in the ordinary course of business and conducted at arm's length, meaning like dealing with an unrelated party, are not bound by these rules.

Disclosures: Every such contract or arrangement must be disclosed in the company's report to shareholders, along with the reasons for entering into it.

Voidable Contracts: If a contract or arrangement with a related party is entered into without proper consent and not ratified within three months, the company has the option to void it. Directors involved must compensate the company for any losses.

Penalties: Directors or employees involved in unauthorized transactions can face penalties, including fines or imprisonment, as outlined in the Act.

Legal Recourse: Companies have the option to take legal action against directors or employees who violate these provisions to recover any losses incurred.

Simplified text: Maximum Managerial Remuneration for Public Companies

1. Total remuneration: The total amount of pay public companies can give to their directors, including managing directors, whole-time directors, and managers, should not exceed eleven percent of the company's net profits in a financial year. This calculation should follow the rules laid out in section 198. The pay of directors should not be subtracted from the company's overall profits. However, with the approval of the Central Government, the company can pay higher remuneration beyond the eleven percent limit, following the guidelines in Schedule V. Without obtaining approval in the general meeting:
   i. The pay for managing directors, whole-time directors, or managers should not exceed five percent of the company's net profits. If there are multiple directors falling under this category, the total remuneration should not surpass ten percent of the net profits for all such directors and manager combined.
   ii. The remuneration for directors who are not managing directors or whole-time directors should be limited to:
A. One percent of the net profits, if there is a managing director, whole-time director, or manager.
B. Three percent of the net profits if none of the above positions exist.

2. Additional fees: The above percentages do not include any fees payable to directors as mentioned in subsection (5).

3. Inadequate profits: If a company has no profits or inadequate profits in a financial year, it should not pay its directors, managing directors, whole-time directors, or managers any remuneration except as outlined in Schedule V. If the company cannot meet these requirements, it must seek the prior approval of the Central Government.

4. Determination of remuneration: The company's articles or a resolution passed by the company in a general meeting should decide the remuneration payable to directors, managing directors, whole-time directors, or managers. The remuneration should cover services rendered in any capacity but exclude professional services if certain conditions are met.

5. Director's fees: Directors can receive remuneration in the form of fees for attending board or committee meetings or for other purposes, with the prescribed maximum limit.

6. Payment methods: Directors or managers can receive remuneration through a monthly payment, a specified percentage of the company's net profits, or a combination of both.

7. Independent directors: Independent directors cannot receive stock options and will be compensated with fees, expense reimbursements, and profit-related commissions approved by the members.

8. Net profits calculation: Net profits should be computed as per section 198.

9. Excess remuneration: If any director receives remuneration exceeding the prescribed limit without approval, they must refund the excess amount to the company.

10. Waiver of recovery: The company cannot forgo the recovery of excess remuneration unless permitted by the Central Government.

11. Compliance with Schedule V: Any provision increasing the directors' remuneration should align with the conditions specified in Schedule V.

12. Disclosure requirement: Listed companies must disclose directors' remuneration ratio to median employee's remuneration and other prescribed details in the Board's report.

13. Insurance premiums: Premiums paid for insurance against liability should not be considered part of remuneration unless the individual is found guilty.

14. Commission from group companies: Directors can receive commission from holding or subsidiary companies, with disclosure in the Board's report.

15. Penalties: Violation of these provisions can result in fines ranging from one lakh to five lakh rupees.

**Calculation of Profits:**

**1. Credit and Deductions:**  
- Calculate the net profits of a company for each financial year according to Section 197.
- Give credit for specified sums under subsection (2) and do not give credit for those under subsection (3).
- Deduct the sums specified in subsection (4) and do not deduct those in subsection (5).

- Credit may be given for bounties and subsidies received from the government or authorized public authorities, unless specified otherwise.

- Deduct usual working charges, directors' remuneration, bonuses or commissions, specified types of taxes, interest payments, repair expenses, contributions, depreciation, excess expenditures, compensation or damages, insurance payments, and bad debts.

**4. Exceptions:**  
- Do not deduct income taxes, compensation not related to liability, losses of a capital nature, or certain changes in asset or liability values.

These are the key elements to consider when calculating profits under the Companies Act, 2013.

Simplified text: Appointment of Key Management Personnel:
Every company of a specific category must appoint the following full-time key management personnel:
- Managing Director, Chief Executive Officer, or Manager, and in their absence, a full-time Director.
- Company Secretary.
- Chief Financial Officer.
An individual cannot serve as both the company's Chairperson and Managing Director or Chief Executive Officer simultaneously, unless:
a. The company's articles state otherwise.
b. The company is not involved in multiple businesses.

The company must appoint each full-time key management personnel through a Board resolution, outlining the terms and conditions, including the salary.
Restrictions:
A full-time key management personnel cannot hold the same position in more than one company simultaneously, except in a subsidiary company. However, with the Board's approval, they may also be a director in another company. If they hold such dual roles at the commencement of this Act, they must select one company within six months to continue as a key management personnel. Additionally, a person can be appointed as a managing director in only one other company with the consent of all present directors and proper notice.
Vacancy Filling:
In case a full-time key management personnel position becomes vacant, the Board must fill the vacancy within six months.
Penalties:
Failure to comply with these regulations may incur fines ranging from one to five lakh rupees for the company, and up to fifty thousand rupees for every director and key management personnel in default. Investigation into Company Affairs by Serious Fraud Investigation Office:

1. Initiation of Investigation:
The Central Government may order an investigation by the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) if it believes such action is necessary:
a. Upon receiving a report from the Registrar or inspector.
b. Upon being informed by a special resolution of a company.
c. In the public interest.
d. Upon request from a Government department.

2. Exclusive Investigation:
Once the Central Government assigns a case to the SFIO, no other investigating agency from the Central or State Government can proceed with that investigation under this Act.
The SFIO should be provided with all documents related to the case.

3. Conducting Investigation:
The SFIO will carry out investigations according to the procedures outlined in this chapter and submit a report to the Central Government within a specified timeframe.

4. Investigative Powers:
The Director of SFIO may appoint inspectors to investigate the company's affairs and has the powers of an inspector under section 217.

5. Cooperation:
The company, its officers, and employees must provide all necessary information, documents, and assistance to the Investigating Officer.

6. Arrest and Offences:
Specific offenses under the Companies Act are cognizable, and accused individuals may not be granted bail without certain conditions.

7. Reporting:
The SFIO must provide interim and final investigation reports to the Central Government.

8. Prosecution:
Based on the investigation report, the Central Government may direct the SFIO to initiate prosecution against the company, its officers, employees, or any related individuals.

9. Legal Proceedings:
The SFIO may share information and documents with other authorized agencies and will continue investigations previously initiated under the Companies Act, 1956.

Simplified text: Procedure and Powers of Inspectors under Companies Act, 2013
Duty of Company Officers:
All officers, employees, agents, and former staff of a company under investigation must:
Preserve and provide all company-related books and papers to an inspector.
Give any reasonable assistance to the inspector during the investigation.

Inspector's Authority:
Inspectors can request information or documents from any company or organization relevant to their investigation.

Duration of Bookkeeping:
Inspectors can keep company documents for a maximum of 180 days and must return them afterward, unless needed further.

Interrogation and Evidence:
Inspectors can question individuals under oath, with permission. They have the authority to demand the presence of any person related to the investigation.

Powers of Inspectors:
Inspectors have the same powers as a civil court under the Civil Procedure Code, 1908. This includes access to accounts, summoning individuals, and examining records.

Officer Non-Compliance:
Failure to assist or provide requested information to an inspector can result in imprisonment or fines. Public agencies must support inspectors when required.

Agreements and International Cooperation:
The Central Government can collaborate with foreign governments to aid investigations. A court may request evidence from abroad, which will be treated as valid evidence in India.

Mutual Legal Assistance:
If evidence from another country is needed, the Central Government can forward a request to the foreign court. The inspector must investigate following the same procedures as domestically.

- Any other company that has been or is currently a subsidiary or holding company of the company under investigation.

Simplified text: Compromise or Arrangement Enforcement
When a Tribunal approves a compromise or arrangement for a company under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, it has the authority to:
- Supervise the implementation of the compromise or arrangement.
- Issue directions or modifications to ensure the proper implementation of the compromise or arrangement, either when the order is made or later on.
If the Tribunal finds that the approved compromise or arrangement cannot be executed successfully, with or without changes, and the company is unable to meet its debts as outlined in the plan, the Tribunal can order the winding up of the company. This order is treated as a new order under the Act.
These rules also apply to companies that had a compromise or arrangement approved before the Companies Act, 2013 came into effect.

**Companies Act, 2013: Merger and Amalgamation of Companies**

1. **Purpose**: When a company wants to merge with or amalgamate with other companies for business reorganization, they must seek approval from the Tribunal. The Tribunal can order a meeting of creditors or members to discuss and approve the scheme.

2. **Procedure for Approval**:
   - Companies must circulate the draft scheme and relevant reports to shareholders and creditors as directed by the Tribunal.
  
3. **Tribunal Approval**:
   - Once the specified procedure is followed, the Tribunal can approve the scheme and make necessary arrangements like:
     - Transferring assets, properties, and liabilities to the receiving company.
     - Issuing shares or instruments to stakeholders as per the scheme.
     - Continuing legal proceedings or dissolving the transferor company without winding up.
     - Addressing dissenting shareholders' concerns and employee transfers.
     
4. **Compliance**:
   - Companies must file the Tribunal's order with the Registrar within 30 days.
   - They must annually submit a compliance report to the Registrar certified by an accounting professional.
  
5. **Penalties**:
   - Non-compliance with the regulations may lead to fines or imprisonment for officers of the companies involved.

**Definitions**:
- **Merger by Absorption**: Existing companies transfer assets and liabilities to another existing company.
- **Merger by Formation of a New Company**: Multiple companies form a new company to transfer assets and liabilities.
- **Division**: Assets and liabilities of a company are divided and transferred among multiple existing or new companies.

By ensuring compliance with the Companies Act, companies can undergo mergers and amalgamations smoothly and efficiently.

Merger and Amalgamation of Companies

1. Small companies or a holding company and its wholly-owned subsidiary can merge or amalgamate under certain conditions:
   a. Notify the scheme to relevant authorities and affected parties for objections and suggestions.
   b. Obtain approval from members holding at least ninety percent of total shares.
   c. Submit a solvency declaration to the Registrar.

7. Registration of the scheme leads to the transfer of property, enforcement of charges, continuation of legal proceedings, and settlement of dissenting shareholders or creditors.

8. The transferee company cannot hold shares in its name after the merger, and all such shares shall be cancelled.

9. The transferee company must update its authorised capital with the Registrar and pay necessary fees.

10. Similar provisions apply to compromise, arrangement, division, or transfer of companies.

11. The Central Government may prescribe rules for the merger or amalgamation of companies.

12. Companies covered under this section can use section 232 for the approval of merger or amalgamation schemes.

Purchase of Minority Shareholding:
1. When a person or group acquires 90% or more of a company's shares, they must inform the company of their intention to buy the remaining shares.
2. The buyer must offer to purchase the minority shareholders' shares at a price determined by a registered valuer.
3. Minority shareholders can also offer to sell their shares to the majority shareholders at the same price.

Companies Amalgamation:

The Central Government has the power to merge two or more companies in the public interest. The Government can issue an order, published in the Official Gazette, to merge these companies into a single entity with specified properties, powers, rights, and obligations.

The order can also address ongoing legal proceedings involving the merging companies and include provisions necessary for the successful merger.

Members and creditors of the merging companies will have similar rights in the new entity as they did in their original companies. If their rights are reduced, they are entitled to compensation assessed by the prescribed authority and published in the Official Gazette.

Any person dissatisfied with the compensation assessment can appeal to the Tribunal within thirty days of its publication in the Official Gazette.

The Central Government cannot finalize the merger order until it has circulated the draft order to the involved companies, considered any modifications suggested by them or other stakeholders, and met certain criteria.

The order made under this section must be presented to both Houses of Parliament promptly following its creation.

Section 242 of Companies Act, 2013

Powers of Tribunal:

If, after receiving an application under section 241, the Tribunal believes:
- the company's affairs harm or might harm a member, public interest, or the company itself.
- winding up the company would unfairly harm a member but a winding-up order is otherwise just, the Tribunal can issue an order to address the issues.
This order can include:
- Regulating future company affairs.
- Selling shares of some members to others or the company.
- Reducing the company's share capital after buying back shares.
- Imposing restrictions on share transfers.
- Changing or ending agreements with directors or managers if deemed fair.
- Cancelling fraudulent transactions made before the application date.
- Removing directors or managers.
- Recovering improper gains from directors or managers and deciding how to use the recovered funds.
- Appointing new directors to report to the Tribunal as directed. 
- Imposing suitable costs, and any other fair measures the Tribunal deems necessary.

Once the Tribunal's order is issued, a certified copy must be filed with the Registrar within thirty days.
The Tribunal can also issue interim orders during proceedings to manage the company's affairs fairly.
If the Tribunal changes the company's memorandum or articles, the company cannot make any inconsistent changes without the Tribunal's permission.
The changes made by the Tribunal will be legally binding as if made by the company.
A certified copy of any order regarding the company's memorandum or articles must be filed with the Registrar within thirty days.
Failure to comply with these rules can result in fines or imprisonment for the company officers.

Simplified text: Removal of Company Names

Registrar's Power: The Registrar can delete a company's name from the register for various reasons, such as:
- Failure to start business within one year of incorporation.
- Non-payment of subscription by initial shareholders within 180 days of incorporation without filing the necessary declaration.
- Not conducting any business for two consecutive financial years without applying to be a dormant company.

Notice and Representation: The Registrar must notify the company and its directors of the intention to remove the company's name. They have 30 days to respond with any relevant documents.

Voluntary Removal: A company can apply to have its name removed by passing a special resolution or with consent from 75% of its shareholders based on paid-up share capital.

Publication: Notice of removal will be published for the public. If there are no objections, the company will be dissolved, but liabilities must be settled.

Appeal Process for Company Restoration

1. An individual who feels unfairly affected by the Registrar's decision to dissolve a company under section 248 can appeal to the Tribunal within three years of the Registrar's order. The Tribunal has the authority to provide necessary directions to reinstate the company and related parties to their pre-removal status.

Determining a Sick Company:
- When secured creditors of a company holding at least fifty percent of its debt demand payment and the company fails to pay within 30 days, a creditor can apply to a Tribunal to declare the company as sick.
- The creditor can also ask for a stay on any winding-up proceedings, property seizures, or receiver appointments.
- The Tribunal can issue an order that lasts for 120 days based on the creditor's application.
- The company can also apply to the Tribunal for similar reasons.
- Government bodies or financial institutions can refer a company to the Tribunal if they believe it is a sick company, with some restrictions.

Company Restrictions:
- When an application is filed, the company cannot dispose of assets except in the normal course of business, and directors cannot act against creditors' interests.

Assessing Repayment:
- If the Tribunal finds that the company is sick, it will determine if the company can repay its debts within a reasonable time.
- If repayment is possible, the Tribunal will allow the company time to do so under specified conditions.

Simplified text: Revival and Rehabilitation of Companies

When a company is declared financially troubled by the Tribunal under section 253, either a secured creditor of the company or the company itself can ask the Tribunal for suggestions on how to revive and rehabilitate the company.

If the majority of secured creditors (representing 75% of the total outstanding amount) start the process to recover their debts under the Securitisation and Reconstruction Act, any ongoing reference or scheme for revival and rehabilitation will be ended.

No new reference can be made if the majority of secured creditors have already initiated debt recovery under the Securitisation and Reconstruction Act.

If a securitization or reconstruction company has acquired the financial assets of the troubled company, no application can be made without the consent of the acquiring company.

The application must include:
- Audited financial statements from the previous financial year.
- Relevant documents and details as required.
- A proposed plan for reviving and rehabilitating the company unless the company declares it has no such plan.

The application must be submitted to the Tribunal within sixty days of the company being declared financially troubled.

Simplified text: Scheme Approval Process:

1. Preparation of Scheme:
   - The administrator of the company will create a scheme.
   - This scheme must be presented to the creditors of the struggling company for their approval in a meeting organized by the administrator within 60 days of their appointment. This period could be extended by the Tribunal up to 120 days.
2. Creditor Approval:
   - Separate meetings will be held for secured and unsecured creditors of the struggling company.
   - If the scheme is approved by unsecured creditors representing one-fourth of the owed amount and secured creditors representing three-fourths of the outstanding financial assistance, the administrator can submit the scheme to the Tribunal for approval.
   - In case of amalgamation with another company, approval from the general meetings of both companies' shareholders is required. The scheme must also be approved by a special resolution passed by the shareholders of that company.
3. Examination and Modifications by Tribunal:
   - The Tribunal will review the scheme and may make necessary modifications.
   - A draft of the modified scheme will be sent to the involved parties for feedback.
4. Sanctioning of Scheme:
   - Once the Tribunal is satisfied with the scheme’s approval process, they will issue an order sanctioning the scheme within 60 days.
5. Implementation of Scheme:
   - If the sanctioned scheme involves the transfer of property or liabilities between companies, the changes will take effect on the designated date.
6. Scheme Review:
   - The Tribunal can review and modify a sanctioned scheme as needed.
7. Legal Standing of Sanctioned Scheme:
   - The Tribunal's approval is considered final proof of compliance with the scheme's requirements.
   - A certified copy of the sanctioned scheme will be admissible as evidence in legal proceedings.
8. Filing of Sanctioned Scheme:
   - The struggling company must file a copy of the sanctioned scheme with the Registrar within 30 days of receipt.

Simplified text: Notification and Committees for Winding up Companies
When the Court issues an order to appoint a provisional liquidator or wind up a company:
- Notification: The Court must inform the Company Liquidator or provisional liquidator and the Registrar within seven days.
- Public Announcement: The Registrar must record and announce the order in the Official Gazette, especially for listed companies, notifying stock exchanges where the company's securities are listed.
- Employee Notice: The winding up order serves as a discharge notice for company officers, employees, and workers unless the company continues its operations.
- Winding up Committee: The Company Liquidator has three weeks to apply to the Court for forming a winding up committee. This committee, consisting of the Official Liquidator, a nominee of secured creditors, and a professional nominated by the Court, will assist in various liquidation tasks:
  - Asset transfer
  - Reviewing financial statements
  - Recovering company assets
  - Auditing company accounts
  - Selling assets
  - Identifying creditors and contributors
  - Handling claims, settlements, and dividends
  - Following any other directions from the Court.
- Progress Report: The Company Liquidator must present monthly reports and committee meeting minutes to the Court until the final dissolution report is submitted.
- Final Report: After the winding up committee approves the final report, the Company Liquidator submits it to the Court for the dissolution order.

The Liquidator may submit further reports if needed.

Creditors or contributors can request to inspect and obtain copies of the report by paying the applicable fee.

5. Other Orders: The Tribunal has the authority to issue any other orders or directions deemed appropriate in the circumstances.

If the Tribunal approves the request and decides to consider the company's revival scheme, the procedures outlined in Chapter XIX will be followed.

Every order made in this regard must be promptly communicated by the Company Liquidator to the Registrar, who will record it in the company's official records.
